title: Writing argumentative essays: should school start later?
summary: Eighth graders learn to write a five-paragraph argumentative essay on school start times. They build a clear claim, reasons, cited evidence, explanations and a counterclaim response from two opinion articles.
brief: Writing argumentative essays for grade 8 English language arts: a three-week unit of fifteen 45-minute lessons. Students learn to state a clear claim, support it with reasons and evidence from two short articles, explain how the evidence supports the claim, answer a counterclaim, and organize a five-paragraph essay with an introduction and a conclusion. The topic is one they care about: should school start later? Use the two attached opinion articles, one for and one against, as the evidence students read, mark up and cite. Build the essay in steps across the unit: a planning organizer, model paragraphs, drafting in class, a peer review session and revision. Grading: the final essay 60% with a rubric, the organizer and drafts 25%, and short quizzes on the terms of argument 15%.
policies:
Bring your writing folder to every class: the organizer, drafts and peer review sheets all stay in it until the final essay is handed in.

Drafts are due on the day set in class. A late draft can still earn full credit if it is finished before peer review, so that your partner has something to read.

Essays use evidence only from the two unit articles, with the article named each time. Copying sentences without quotation marks, from the articles or anywhere else, is plagiarism.

l_f748df4def98.summary: Students meet the question of later school start times and learn the basic terms of argument through short, familiar debates.

segments.title: Stand where you stand: choosing seats
segments.description:
Pose the question: “Should students choose their own seats in class?” Students move to the Yes side or the No side of the room.
Each side gives one reason out loud, and the teacher writes both on the board.
Point out that everyone already argues this way.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep it light and fast. If students only say “because I want to,” ask “What would you tell the principal?” Do not correct reasons yet. Return to the board list in the next segment.

segments.title: Claim, reason, evidence
segments.description:
Use the seating debate to name the parts: the position is the claim, and the why is the reason.
Show the opening lines of “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” on the board. Its claim is “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”
Model the chain: one reason is that later starts help students sleep more. The evidence is Torres’s report that students in the Seattle study slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their schools moved the start time later.
Students copy the three terms into notes, each in their own words.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress that evidence answers “How do we know?” Show the chain as three stacked boxes. Misconception: students call any strong opinion evidence. Test with “Is this something that can be checked?” The articles are read in full later in the unit.

segments.title: Sort the statements: claim or reason
segments.description:
Pairs get six statements on cards and sort them into Claim and Reason.
They match each reason to the claim it supports.
Pairs then explain one match to another pair.
segments.teacherNotes:
Statements and answers:
1. Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Claim
2. Later starts help students get enough sleep. Reason, supports 1
3. Students should have a longer lunch period. Claim
4. A longer lunch gives students time to eat and rest. Reason, supports 3
5. A later start would cause transportation problems. Reason, supports 6
6. Schools should not move the start time. Claim
Common mistake: calling a reason a claim because it sounds strong. Ask “Does this statement give the position on the school policy, or explain why someone should accept that position?”

segments.title: Build a mini argument
segments.description:
Pairs choose a side on the question “Should school start later?”
They write one claim and one reason, then say aloud what evidence would convince a doubter.
Three pairs share, and the class names each part they hear.
segments.teacherNotes: Students have not read the articles yet, so accept ideas such as “we could survey our grade.” Do not let anyone state invented statistics as fact. Prompt with “Suppose a survey of our school found…” Both sides are welcome; many students will favor a later start.

segments.title: Exit check in your own words
segments.description:
On a slip, each student defines claim, reason and evidence in their own words.
They then label three statements as claim, reason or evidence.
Collect the slips as a quick check of the first two objectives.
segments.teacherNotes:
Ungraded. Sort slips into got it and needs review, and revisit the second pile at the start of next time. Statements and answers:
1. Schools should teach students about sleep. Claim
2. Sleep education costs little. Reason
3. In Seattle, researchers found students slept about half an hour longer on school nights after the start time moved. Evidence

segments.title: Back to the big question
segments.description:
Each student finishes the sentence “My first guess about the school start time is… because…”
Preview that next time they will read an article for a later start and mark its claim, reasons and evidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Tell students that first guesses can change after reading. Keep their sentences to compare with their views after both articles are read.

keyIdeas: An argument is a claim backed by reasons, and the reasons are backed by evidence.
A claim is a position someone could disagree with. A reason says why the claim is right.
Evidence is a fact, example or expert statement that shows the reason is true.
The question of whether school should start later has strong support on both sides, and we will read both sides later in the unit.

study.overview: An argument is a claim backed by reasons, and the reasons are backed by evidence. In this lesson you used the question of whether school should start later, along with a seating debate, to name each part and tell the parts apart. Later in the unit you will read an article for each side of the school start time question. Knowing these three terms will help you mark up what you read and build your own argument.

points.heading: A claim is a position someone could disagree with
points.explanation: A claim is the position a writer wants you to accept. It takes a side, so a person could disagree with it. The first article’s claim is: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Another student could argue the opposite, so it works as a claim. A claim about our own debate would be: “Students should choose their own seats in class.” Ask yourself: does this statement give a position on a policy? If yes, it is probably a claim.

points.heading: A reason says why the claim is right
points.explanation: A reason explains why someone should accept the claim. It does not take the position itself. It answers “Why?” For the claim “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later,” one reason is: “Later starts help students get enough sleep.” Another pair of statements shows the same link. The claim “Students should have a longer lunch period” is supported by the reason “A longer lunch gives students time to eat and rest.” A reason can sound strong and still be a reason, not a claim. Check whether it explains why a position is right instead of stating the position.

points.heading: Evidence shows the reason is true
points.explanation: Evidence is a fact, an example or an expert statement that shows a reason is true. It answers “How do we know?” A strong opinion is not evidence. Test it by asking, “Is this something that can be checked?” Here is the chain from the lesson. Claim: our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Reason: later starts help students sleep more. Evidence: in Seattle, researchers found students slept about half an hour longer on school nights after the start time moved. You can picture the chain as three stacked boxes, with the evidence holding up the reason and the reason holding up the claim.

points.heading: Both sides of this question have strong support
points.explanation: People who want a later start and people who want to keep the schedule can each build a full argument. A claim for one side might be “Schools should not move the start time.” A reason for it is “A later start would cause transportation problems.” Later in the unit you will read both sides, so keep your first guess about the school start time and compare it with your view after you read. First guesses can change. When you think of evidence for your own ideas, do not make up numbers. If you need an idea, you can say, “Suppose a survey of our school found...” to show that it is only an example.

l_6032d5e8f353.title: Reading the case for a later start
l_6032d5e8f353.summary: Students read and annotate Maya Torres's article, marking her claim, her three main reasons and the evidence behind each.
readings: Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, by Maya Torres

segments.title: First look: what does the author want us to do?
segments.description:
Hand out printed copies of Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later. Students read the first paragraph silently.
On a sticky note, each student writes one sentence: “Maya Torres wants our school to… because…”.
Two volunteers read their sentences aloud. The class compares them to the “My first guess… because…” sentences from last time.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect answers like “start at 8:30 because teens are tired.” Accept any that name a position and a why. Collect the sticky notes to see who found the claim easily.

segments.title: Model: marking the claim and the first reason
segments.description:
Project the first four paragraphs of the article. Teach one set of marks: box the claim, circle and number each reason, underline evidence.
Think aloud: box “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later” as the claim.
Circle “First, teenagers need more sleep than most of them get” as reason 1. Underline “8 to 10 hours of sleep every night” and the 6:45 a.m. bus example as evidence.
Ask the class to find one more fact to underline in the paragraph about the American Academy of Pediatrics.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: boxing the whole first paragraph. The boxed words state the position; the rest of that sentence previews the reasons. Also underline “2014” and “fewer than one in five” as numbers. Students copy the marks onto their own printed copy.

segments.title: Annotate reasons two and three in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs annotate the rest of the article with the same marks: circle and number reasons 2 and 3, underline evidence.
Tell them to look for signal words at the start of paragraphs and to write a note in the margin saying what each underline proves.
Pairs finish by listing, on the back of the page, the three reasons in their own words.
Circulate and ask: “Is this a fact you could check, or the writer’s opinion?”
segments.teacherNotes: Reason 2: students sleep more when school starts later; evidence is Seattle in 2016, 7:50 to 8:45 a.m., a little over half an hour more sleep, grades up in biology classes. Reason 3: sleep affects more than grades; it has few numbers. Students may underline the California law, which belongs to the answer to objections. Allow it, then redirect.

segments.title: Which reason has the strongest evidence?
segments.description:
Pairs join another pair and compare their underlining.
Each group chooses the reason with the strongest evidence and the one with the weakest, and explains why in one sentence.
Three groups share with the class. The class votes with hands on which reason is best supported.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely consensus: reason 2 is strongest (named city, year, numbers); reason 3 is weakest (general statements, no numbers). Praise answers that point to numbers or named experts. Do not require the class to agree with Torres, only to judge her support.

segments.title: Exit check: evidence or not evidence?
segments.description:
Display four sentences from the article. On a slip, each student writes E for evidence or N for not evidence beside each one.
Students add a few words explaining one of their choices.
Collect the slips as they leave the check.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. “Many of them are not lazy.” N, the writer’s opinion.
2. “people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night” E, expert statement with numbers.
3. “Those problems are real, but they can be solved.” N, a judgment, not a checkable fact.
4. “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights” E, Seattle result.

segments.title: Looking ahead to the other side
segments.description:
Students complete the sentence: “Torres’s best evidence is… because…”.
Tell the class that next time they will read the article written against a later start and mark it with the same symbols.
Students keep their annotated copy in their folder for later in the unit, when they choose evidence to cite.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students to keep the annotated article. They will reuse it when choosing and citing evidence for their essay. Nothing here is graded unless you choose to check the folders.

The hormone in the brain that makes people sleepy; in teenagers it is released later in the evening.

study.overview: In class you read Maya Torres’s article, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, and marked it with the same symbols every time. Her claim is in the first paragraph: our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. She gives three reasons and backs them with evidence. Marking the article this way makes the argument easy to find again when you write your own essay.

points.heading: Find the claim and the three reasons
points.explanation: The claim is the position the writer wants you to accept. Torres states it in her first paragraph: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Box only those words. The rest of the sentence, “because later start times help students sleep enough, learn better and stay healthier,” previews her reasons, so it is not part of the claim. Her three reasons begin with signal words. Reason 1: teenagers need more sleep than most of them get. Reason 2: students sleep more when schools start later. Reason 3: sleep supports health and safety as well as grades. Circle and number each one.

points.heading: Underline the evidence behind each reason
points.explanation: Evidence is a fact, number or expert statement that you could check. Torres’s strongest evidence is specific. For reason 1, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine says people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. Her example of a student catching a 6:45 a.m. bus adds a time. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation in 2014 and the finding that fewer than one in five schools start that late are numbers too. For reason 2, Seattle high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights, and grades went up in the biology classes studied. In the margin, write what each underline proves.

points.heading: Tell evidence from opinion
points.explanation: Not every sentence is evidence. Opinions and appeals to feeling are not facts you can check. “Many of them are not lazy” is the writer’s opinion, so it is not evidence. “Those problems are real, but they can be solved” is a judgment, not a checkable fact. Compare these with “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.” That is a Seattle result, so it is evidence. When you are unsure, ask: could I check this, or is it what the writer believes?

points.heading: Judge which reason is best supported
points.explanation: You can judge how well a writer supports a reason without agreeing with her. Reason 2 is the strongest because it names a city, a year and numbers. Reason 3 is the weakest because it makes general statements and gives no numbers. Keep your annotated article in your folder. Later in the unit you will use it to choose evidence for your own essay.

l_2aaf5297ff5d.title: Reading the case against a later start
l_2aaf5297ff5d.summary: Students annotate Daniel Okafor's article and compare its problems and counterarguments with the claims in Torres's piece.
readings: A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems, by Daniel Okafor

segments.title: Torres’s claim, then the other side
segments.description:
Students take out their annotated copy of Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later from last time.
Pairs tell each other Torres’s claim and her best evidence, using their last sentence: ‘Torres’s best evidence is… because…’.
Then each student writes one guess on a slip: ‘A later start could cause this problem: …’.
Students keep the slip for the close.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Torres wants school to start at 8:30 a.m. or later; best evidence is often the Seattle results or the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation. Guesses may include buses, sports and jobs. Do not correct them yet.

segments.title: Model: marking Okafor’s claim and first problem
segments.description:
Hand out printed copies of A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems, by Daniel Okafor, and project the first two paragraphs.
Use the same marks as last time: box the claim, circle and number each reason, underline evidence.
Think aloud as you box ‘moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like’. Ask students why this claim is harder to spot than Torres’s.
Circle and number the transportation problem as 1, and underline the detail that the same buses make several trips each morning.
segments.teacherNotes: Okafor’s claim is less direct than Torres’s: he argues against a change rather than for one. The closing paragraph restates it: look honestly at the costs before changing. Misconception: that he disagrees about sleep. He agrees teens need 8 to 10 hours.

segments.title: Annotate problems two and three in pairs
segments.description:
Pairs annotate the rest of Okafor’s article with the same marks.
They circle and number problem 2 (after school) and problem 3 (family schedules), and underline the evidence for each.
They also bracket the paragraph where Okafor discusses Seattle, and the paragraph about other ways to help students sleep.
Pairs then write the three problems in a short phrase each at the top of the page.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: problem 2 is after school (sports daylight, part-time jobs, caring for siblings); problem 3 is family schedules (parents leaving early). Common mistake: circling the Seattle paragraph as a fourth reason. It answers Torres’s evidence. Circulate and check marks match last time’s.

segments.title: Compare how the two articles use evidence
segments.description:
Pairs fill a four-row chart with one column for Torres and one for Okafor.
The rows are: the claim, the kind of evidence, the numbers given, and how each uses Seattle.
Then discuss as a class: which details in each article give evidence you could check, and which describe possible effects?
Students point to an underlined line to back each answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Row answers. Claim: Torres says start at 8:30 a.m. or later; Okafor says a later start is not an easy fix. Kind: Torres uses experts, numbers and Seattle; Okafor uses mostly explained possibilities. Numbers: Torres gives many; Okafor few. Seattle: Torres uses it as evidence supporting a later start; Okafor says one city may not predict others. Note both agree on about half an hour more sleep.

segments.title: Exit check: evidence or not evidence?
segments.description:
Display four sentences from Okafor’s article.

study.overview: In this lesson you read Daniel Okafor’s article, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” and marked it up the same way you marked Maya Torres’s article last time. Okafor agrees that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. He disagrees that moving the school day later is the simple answer. You found his claim and his three problems. Then you compared how he and Torres use evidence. Keep both annotated articles, because you will cite them in your essay later in the unit.

points.heading: Okafor’s claim and his three problems
points.explanation: Okafor’s claim is that moving the school day later is “not the simple answer it sounds like.” He states it in the first paragraph and returns to it in the last, where he says the school should look honestly at the costs before it changes its start time. His claim is harder to spot than Torres’s because he argues against a change instead of for one. Do not think he disagrees about sleep: he says teenagers need 8 to 10 hours. He gives three problems, and each one is a reason for his position. Problem 1 is transportation. The same buses make several trips each morning, so a later high school start means buying more buses or sending younger children earlier. Problem 2 is what happens after school. A school day that ends at 4:00 p.m. instead of 3:00 p.m. leaves sports teams less daylight and cuts the hours of students with part-time jobs. Problem 3 is family schedules. Parents who leave for work early may no longer be able to drop their teenagers at school on the way.

points.heading: Two kinds of evidence
points.explanation: Torres and Okafor do not support their claims in the same way. Torres uses expert statements, numbers and the Seattle results. For example, she gives the 8 to 10 hours recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the 2014 recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics. Okafor mostly explains what could happen, and he gives few numbers. His sentence “Instead, the same buses make several trips each morning: one for the high school, then the middle school, then the elementary schools” is evidence, because it describes how the system works and a reader could check it. His sentence “Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark” is not evidence. It gives a feeling from unnamed people. His sentence “A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves” is not evidence either. It is an opinion. When you read, ask whether a detail is something you could check or only a possible effect. Point to the underlined line that proves your answer.

points.heading: How both writers use the Seattle study
points.explanation: Both writers use the Seattle study, but for different purposes. In 2016, Seattle’s high schools moved their start time later, and researchers found that students slept about half an hour more on school nights. Both articles agree on that result. Torres uses it as evidence that a later start works. Okafor calls it “a real result” and then says it came from one city with its own buses, budgets and families, so it might not work the same way somewhere else. Notice that Okafor’s Seattle paragraph is not a fourth reason. It answers Torres’s evidence. Also notice what he does with the words “That is a real result.” This is called conceding a point: he admits something is true, then answers it. A writer who does this can make an argument stronger, because readers see that the writer has weighed the other side fairly. You will use this idea when you write your own response to a counterclaim.

segments.title: Whose claim is clearer?

Display the claims of the two writers from the articles students have already annotated. Torres: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Okafor: “moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like.”
Students tell a partner what each writer wants the school to do.
Take two or three answers and ask which claim makes the action easier to name.

segments.title: The three-part test for a claim

Write three questions on the board: Does it take a side? Is it specific about who should do what? Could someone argue against it?
Model the test on one weak claim, “School start times are a big issue.” It names a topic but takes no side.
Revise it on the board in two steps: first “Schools should start later,” then “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”
After each step, rerun the three questions aloud and tick the ones that now pass.

2. “In 2016, Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.” Fact: it reports a checkable event described in Torres’s article. It could serve as evidence.
3. “Early school is bad.” Vague: takes a side, but who and what should change?
4. “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Clear claim.
5. “Our school should keep its current start time.” Clear claim.

segments.title: Revise a vague claim

Pairs rewrite three vague claims into specific claims that pass all three questions of the test.
Pairs then swap papers with another pair. The new pair applies the test and marks any question the revision still fails.
Pairs fix anything flagged.
segments.teacherNotes:
Vague claims and sample revisions (accept any that pass the test):
1. “School start times are a problem.” Revision: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”
2. “A later start is bad.” Revision: “Our school should not move its start time later.”
3. “Sleep is important for students.” Revision: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later so students have more opportunity to get the 8 to 10 hours of sleep that teenagers need.”
Watch for students who simply add “I think.”

segments.title: Write your own claim
segments.description:
Each student recalls their first guess about school start times from before reading the articles. They also review their annotated copies of both articles.
They write a claim about their school’s start time on the first line of a planning organizer page.
They test it with the three questions and revise it once.
segments.teacherNotes: Students may change sides after reading both articles. Let them. Circulate and check three things: a side is chosen, the claim names the school, and it states the action (a time, or keeping the current time). This claim goes into the organizer, which counts toward the organizer and drafts grade (25%).

segments.title: Exit check: my claim

They finish: “My claim passes the test because…”

segments.teacherNotes: Read slips to find claims that still lack a side or an action. Return those with one question, such as “What should the school do?” Students keep their final claim for later in the unit, when they add reasons, evidence and a counterclaim response.

points.heading: A strong claim takes a side and says what should happen
points.explanation: A claim is not a topic and not a feeling. It tells the reader what you want done, and a reasonable person could disagree with it. Maya Torres writes, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” That takes a side and names an action. Daniel Okafor argues that “moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like.” That is a real position, but it is less specific about what the school should do. Compare it with a claim such as “Our school should keep its current start time,” which names the action.

points.heading: Use the three-question test
points.explanation: Ask three questions about any claim. Does it take a side? Is it specific about who should do what? Could someone argue against it? Take the weak statement “School start times are a big issue.” It names a topic but takes no side, so it fails. Revise it to “Schools should start later.” Now it takes a side, but it still does not say which schools or what time. Revise again to “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Now it passes all three questions. Notice that the final claim is short but exact. A longer claim is not automatically a better claim.

points.heading: Tell facts, vague statements and clear claims apart
points.explanation: A fact reports something that can be checked. “In 2016, Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.” is a fact from Torres’s article. It does not say what should happen, so it is not a claim. But it can work later as evidence to support a claim. A vague statement is missing a side, an action, or both. “Start times are interesting” has no side and no action. “Early school is bad” takes a side, but it does not say who should change what. A clear claim takes a side and names an action, such as “Our school should keep its current start time.”

points.heading: Revise a vague claim by making it specific

A revision is “Our school should not move its start time later.” “Sleep is important for students” is true, but it asks for no action. segments.title: Find Torres’s three reasons again

segments.title: The reason test
segments.description:
Write three questions on the board: Is it about this claim? If it is true, does it make the claim more believable? Is it different from my other reasons?
Model with the claim “Students should choose their own seats.” Think aloud as you test the reason “Students pay attention better when they sit where they feel comfortable.” Then test “The chairs are made of plastic.”

They test each reason with the three questions and cross out and rewrite any that fail.

segments.title: Back to the big question

On an exit slip, each student writes the three final reasons under their claim.
Tell students they will find evidence for each reason next time.

study.overview: A reason tells your reader why your claim is right. One reason is rarely enough, so a strong claim has about three, and each one should be different from the others. Before you keep a reason, test it with three questions. In class you used the test to keep or reject reasons for Torres’s claim, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Then you used it on your own reasons.

points.heading: A reason says why, and a claim needs more than one
points.explanation: A claim is your position. A reason answers the question “Why should anyone agree?” Torres gives three different reasons for her claim: teenagers need more sleep than most of them get; students sleep more when schools start later; and sleep helps health and safety as well as grades. Each one backs the same claim in a different way. Okafor does the same on the other side with three problems: transportation, after-school schedules and family schedules. A reason is not the same as evidence. The Seattle numbers are evidence that supports a reason. They are not a reason themselves. You will find evidence for each of your reasons next time.

points.heading: The reason test: three questions
points.explanation: Ask these questions about every reason. First, is it about this claim? Second, if it is true, does it make the claim more believable? Third, is it different from my other reasons? A reason that passes all three stays. A reason that fails any one is rejected. Try it with the claim “Students should choose their own seats.” The reason “Students pay attention better when they sit where they feel comfortable” passes. It is about seats, and if it is true, a reader is more likely to agree. Now compare it with “Choosing seats lets students sit where they feel comfortable and pay attention.” That is the same reason in new words, so it fails question 3.

points.heading: A true statement can still fail
points.explanation: Many students think a true statement is always a good reason. It is not. Take “The chairs are made of plastic.” It may be true, but it does not explain why students should choose their own seats. It fails question 2. Other kinds of failure show up in the cards from class. “Our cafeteria food is bad” is off topic and fails question 1. “School should start later because school should not start so early” only repeats the claim and fails question 2. “Many students like to sleep in on weekends” does not, by itself, explain why school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, so it also fails question 2. Compare these with reasons that pass: “Rested teenagers are safer drivers” and “Students who sleep more can pay attention better.”

points.heading: Test your own three reasons
points.explanation: Your reasons can support either side of the debate. Write each reason as a complete sentence under your claim. Then run each one through the three questions, and cross out and rewrite any that fail. Check especially that no two reasons say the same thing in different words. A student who opposes a later start could use Okafor’s three problems: transportation, after-school schedules and family schedules. These are three different reasons, not one reason said three times. When you check a partner’s reasons, judge only whether each reason supports the claim, not whether you agree with the position.

segments.title: Which would convince a skeptical friend?

Display two statements about teenage sleep: a general one written for this warm-up, and a close paraphrase of a sentence from Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later. Students pick the one that would better convince a skeptical friend that teenagers need more sleep than most get.
Take two or three quick answers and ask what made the choice.
Say that today they learn to judge evidence, not just find it.

Statement A (written for the warm-up, not from the article): “Lots of teenagers are tired in the morning.” Expected: not chosen, because it is general and gives no source or measurement to support it.
Statement B (paraphrase of Torres): “The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says people from 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.” Expected: chosen, because it names a group, ages and numbers. Do not say it is proven yet.

segments.title: Model: three labels for evidence
segments.description:
Write three labels on the board: Reliable, Relevant only, Weak. Under them write three questions: Does it fit this reason? Does it give source clues? Could a reader check it?
Project the Seattle sentences from Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, with the reason “Students sleep more when schools start later.” Think aloud as you add one new mark to the annotation marks: a star above each source clue (2016, Seattle, University of Washington, before and after).
Label it Reliable. Say that clues let a reader trace and check evidence, but the articles alone cannot prove it is accurate.
segments.teacherNotes: Check fit first: evidence that does not fit the reason is Weak for that reason, however trustworthy its source. Reliable: fits the reason and names a source a reader can trust and trace, such as experts or a measured study. Relevant only: fits but names no source. Weak: off the reason, opinion, or nothing to check. Stress that clues are not proof. Accuracy needs another source, such as the study itself. Students keep using last time’s reason test for the “fit” question.

segments.title: Sort six pieces of evidence
segments.description:
Pairs get six evidence cards from both articles, three for each reason. The reasons are “Teenagers need more sleep than most get” (Torres) and “A later start would create transportation problems” (Okafor).
For each card, pairs apply the three questions, write Reliable, Relevant only or Weak, and star any source clues.
Pairs write one sentence of why on their two hardest cards.
Walk the room and listen for the three questions.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards, one per line with answer:
1. “Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine say that people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.” Reliable (group, ages, numbers).
2. “That is why many teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m.” Relevant only (fits, no named source).
3. “Many of them are not lazy. They are tired, and science can explain why.” Weak support (general assertions with no specific finding or source).
4. “Many school districts do not have enough buses and drivers to take every student to school at the same time.” Relevant only (fits, no district or number).
5. “Games against schools with different schedules become harder to plan.” Weak for transportation (about after-school, not buses).
6. “Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark.” Weak (“many people,” opinion).
Common mistake: calling card 1 proven. Say it is traceable.

segments.title: One study, two uses
segments.description:
Project the Seattle passages from both articles side by side. Pairs discuss two questions: What does the Seattle evidence show? What does it not show?
Hear from three pairs.
Ask how Okafor’s line “That is a real result” fits with his point about one city.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: it shows Seattle students slept about half an hour more on school nights, and both writers report this. It does not show the same result in every town. Okafor limits how far it reaches. He does not cancel the finding. Both articles agree, but checking accuracy still needs the original study.

segments.title: Choose evidence for my own reason
segments.description:
Each student picks one reason from their reasons sheet from last time. Explain that this work prepares the graded Organizer and drafts component.
They find two pieces of evidence for it in either article, copy each onto the sheet, and star the source clues.
They label each piece Reliable, Relevant only or Weak and write one sentence of why.
Students who find no strong evidence note which kind of evidence they would still need.
segments.teacherNotes: Students keep these sheets for use later in the unit. Common mistakes: choosing evidence that fits a different reason, or labeling by whether they agree with it. Remind them that the label is about the evidence, not the side. Reasons with no strong evidence in the articles are a useful finding.

segments.title: Exit check: rate two sentences
segments.description:
Display each sentence with the paragraph around it: Okafor’s Seattle paragraph for Sentence 1 and Torres’s Seattle paragraph for Sentence 2. Students may use those paragraphs when identifying source clues. Students test them against the reason “Students sleep more when schools start later.”
On a slip, each student writes Reliable, Relevant only or Weak for each sentence, with one sentence of why.
Collect the slips.
segments.teacherNotes:
Sentence 1: “A change that worked in Seattle might not work the same way somewhere else.” Expected: Weak for this reason. It identifies a limit on applying the Seattle finding elsewhere; it does not itself provide evidence that students sleep more.
Sentence 2: “They found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.” Expected: Reliable (Seattle, University of Washington, before and after measurement).
Accept answers with sound reasons.

keyIdeas: Strong evidence fits a specific reason. A fact can be true and still be the wrong evidence for the reason it is attached to.

Source clues show where evidence comes from: a named group, a year, a place, a measurement. Clues let a reader trace and check the evidence. They do not prove it is accurate, and the two articles alone cannot confirm accuracy.

Check two things in order. First, relevance: does it fit the reason? Evidence that does not fit is weak for that reason, however trustworthy its source. Second, reliability: does it name a source a reader can trust and trace? Evidence that fits and names such a source is reliable; evidence that fits but names no source is relevant only.

Describes evidence a reader has good reason to trust. Consider the source’s expertise and how the information was gathered. Source clues, such as a named expert group or a measured study, are what let a reader judge reliability. Reliable evidence is trusted, not proven.
True and correct. A reader cannot confirm accuracy from the articles alone and must check the original source.
A statement that does not show the reason is true. It may be off the reason, only an opinion, or have nothing a reader can check.

segments.title: Who says so?
segments.description:
Display this sentence: “Students in Seattle slept more after school started later.”
Ask: “Could a reader check this? What is missing?”
Then display a second version: “According to Maya Torres, scientists from the University of Washington found that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
Pairs say which version they would trust and why.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the first version names no source, so a reader cannot tell where the information came from. The second says who found it and gives the amount. Link to last time, when we judged evidence by whether it names a source.

segments.title: Signal phrases and the quote-or-paraphrase choice
segments.description:
Project three ways to bring in evidence from one paragraph of Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, the paragraph about the body’s clock.
A signal phrase: “According to Torres,” and “Torres points out that”.
A quotation: Torres writes, “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.”
A paraphrase: Torres explains that during puberty the body’s clock shifts later, so many teenagers are not sleepy until about 11 p.m.
Students copy two rules: quote when the exact words are the point, and paraphrase when the idea is the point.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the full name, Maya Torres, the first time and Torres after that. Put a comma after “According to Torres.” Do not put a comma after “Torres points out that.” Use a comma before a quotation introduced by “Torres writes.” Quotation marks mean the words are exact. Verbs to post: says, explains, points out, argues, reports.

segments.title: Model: paraphrasing one sentence
segments.description:
Project this sentence from Torres: “A student who must catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. would have to fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get even eight hours.”
Model four steps aloud: read it, cover it, say it in your own words, then check the meaning against the original.
Write the result with a signal phrase: “According to Torres, getting eight hours of sleep means being asleep around 9:30 p.m. for a student whose bus arrives at 6:45 a.m.”
Students say what stayed the same: the times, the hours and the author.
segments.teacherNotes: Two bad versions to show. Too close: “Torres says a student who has to catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. must fall asleep by 9:30 p.m. to get eight hours.” Changed meaning: “Torres says teenagers cannot sleep before 9:30 p.m.”

segments.title: Quote or paraphrase? Four sentences from Torres

Pairs get a handout with four sentences from Torres’s article.
For each, they decide whether to quote or paraphrase and circle the choice.
Then they write the sentence with a signal phrase naming Torres.
Pairs trade handouts and check each other’s work for the author’s name, exact words inside quotation marks, and unchanged meaning.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers (wording of answers will vary):
1. “Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine say that people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.” Paraphrase: Torres reports that sleep experts say teenagers aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours nightly.
2. “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.” Quote: Torres writes, “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.”
3. “They found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.” Paraphrase: Torres reports that University of Washington researchers found that Seattle students gained slightly more than thirty minutes of sleep on school nights.
4. “If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.” Quote: Torres concludes, “If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.”
Mistake to watch: item 3 starts with “They”; students must name the researchers.

segments.description:
Display this sentence from Torres: “Tired students have a harder time paying attention, controlling their moods and making safe choices.”
Each student writes one paraphrase with a signal phrase naming Torres on an exit slip.
Students hand in the slip.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: “Torres argues that students who are tired struggle to focus, manage their feelings and decide safely.” Look for the author’s name, no quotation marks, and the same three effects. Slips show who needs help before the drafting steps later in the unit.

Students take out the reasons sheet and the evidence they chose last time.

Students keep the sheet in their folder for the planning organizer, which belongs to the organizer and drafts grade.

A paraphrase puts the author’s idea in your own words and your own sentence shape. Use one when the idea matters more than the wording.
A good paraphrase keeps the meaning exactly and still names the author. Swapping a few words, or changing what the author said, does not count.

Put a comma before a quotation that follows “Torres writes.” For example: Torres writes, “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.” The comparison is vivid, so the exact words work better than a summary. points.heading: Paraphrase when the idea is the point
points.explanation: A paraphrase puts the author’s idea in your own words and your own sentence shape. Use four steps: read the sentence, cover it, say it in your own words, then check the meaning against the original. Original: “A student who must catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. would have to fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get even eight hours.” Good paraphrase: According to Torres, getting eight hours of sleep means being asleep around 9:30 p.m. for a student whose bus arrives at 6:45 a.m. The times, the hours and the author all stayed the same. A paraphrase still needs the author’s name and has no quotation marks.

points.heading: Avoid two common paraphrase mistakes
points.explanation: The first mistake is staying too close to the original: “Torres says a student who has to catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. must fall asleep by 9:30 p.m. to get eight hours.” Only a few words changed, so this is not a real paraphrase. The second mistake is changing the meaning: “Torres says teenagers cannot sleep before 9:30 p.m.” Torres did not say that. Also watch for a sentence that begins with “They.” If the original says “They found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer,” your version must name the researchers, such as the University of Washington scientists, and still credit Torres. Another example to try: “Torres argues that students who are tired struggle to focus, manage their feelings and decide safely.”

l_11b7070e1c85.title: Explaining how evidence supports the claim

segments.title: Evidence with no explanation
segments.description:
Display Torres’s claim: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”
Beneath it, display this evidence: According to Torres, Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time moved later.
Students write one sentence on a slip: “If I were the reader, what would I still want to know?”
Take two or three answers aloud and write the common question on the board: So what? Why does this help the claim?
segments.teacherNotes: Expect answers like “Is half an hour a lot?” or “What does that have to do with school time?” Praise them: that gap is what commentary fills. Students keep the slip for the close.

segments.title: Evidence plus commentary
segments.description:
Show the Seattle evidence again and add two commentary sentences beneath it, building them one step at a time.
Step one: say what the evidence shows. Step two: say why that matters. Step three: tie back to the claim in your own words.
Put three sentence starters on the board: “This shows that...”, “This matters because...”, “So a later start would...”
Then build the same three steps with the bus costs from A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems, with students suggesting the wording.
segments.teacherNotes: Model for Seattle: “The extra sleep matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours each night, and sleeping longer brings them closer to that amount. This supports starting school later because the Seattle result suggests that changing the schedule can help students get more rest.” Bus model: According to Okafor, a district might need to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. Commentary: If the district buys more buses, it has less money available for teachers or books. This supports examining transportation costs before changing the start time because the change could reduce money available for classroom needs. Stress own words. Do not copy the claim word for word.

segments.title: Spot the missing explanation
segments.description:
Pairs get four short model paragraph excerpts, each with evidence and the sentences that follow it.
For each one, they write Explained or Missing. If it is missing, they underline where the explanation should go and write what the reader still needs to know.
Go over the answers as a class and ask which sentence starter would fix each Missing one.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. According to Torres, Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Another reason is that tired students struggle to pay attention. Answer: Missing; no sentences link the Seattle result to the claim.
2. Same Seattle evidence, then: This matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours, and 30 more minutes moves them closer to that. So a later start would help students get the sleep they need. Answer: Explained.
3. According to Okafor, a district might need to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. If the district buys more buses, that money cannot pay for teachers or books. This supports examining costs before changing the schedule because a later start could leave less money for classroom needs. Answer: Explained.
4. Same Seattle evidence, then: Students slept more in Seattle. They slept longer on school nights. Answer: Missing; it only repeats the evidence. Common mistake: counting any sentence after evidence as commentary.

segments.title: Write commentary for my own evidence
segments.description:
Students take out the reasons sheet and the cited evidence with a signal phrase from last time.
Under their cited evidence, they write two sentences of commentary in their own words. The first says why the evidence matters. The second ties it back to their claim.
Students who finish write commentary for a second piece of evidence.
Circulate and ask each student the question: So what?
segments.teacherNotes: Students keep the sentences with their planning organizer and body paragraph drafts, which count toward Organizer and drafts (25%). Support: give struggling writers the three sentence starters. Watch for commentary that repeats the claim word for word or repeats the evidence. Ask for “because” or “so” to push the thinking.

segments.title: Partner test for commentary
segments.description:
Partners swap sheets and read each other’s evidence and two sentences.
The reader checks three things: Does it say why the evidence matters? Is it in the writer’s own words? Does it tie back to the claim?
The reader marks one strong word or phrase and one place that needs more explanation.
Writers revise one sentence using the feedback.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind readers to check against the claim on the sheet, not their own opinion. If partners disagree on a sentence, the writer reads it aloud and the reader answers the question: So what?

segments.title: Exit check: add the missing explanation
segments.description:
Display this evidence paragraph ending: According to Torres, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
On an exit slip, students write one sentence of commentary that explains why this supports Torres’s claim.
segments.teacherNotes: Strong answers say why a recommendation from children’s doctors makes the claim more believable, for example: doctors who study children’s health agree, so the claim is not just opinion. Weak answers repeat the recommendation. Sort slips into ready and needs more help.

segments.title: Back to the So what? question
segments.description:
Students look at the question they wrote on their warm-up slip.
Ask volunteers whether their commentary now answers it.
Preview that next time they will answer a counterclaim, using the same habit of explaining.
segments.teacherNotes: Collect the exit slips at the door. Keep the examples of strong commentary, with names removed, for use later in the unit when students draft body paragraphs.

keyIdeas: Evidence does not explain itself. After a quotation or paraphrase, the writer adds commentary that tells the reader why the evidence supports the claim.

Different pieces of evidence need commentary that connects them to the writer’s claim. The Seattle result supports Torres’s claim about sleep, while Okafor’s bus costs support his claim about new problems.
A reader can spot missing explanation by asking: after the evidence, does the writer say why it matters to the claim?

study.overview: Evidence does not explain itself. After you give a quotation or a paraphrase, your reader may still ask, “So what? Why does this help the claim?” Commentary is the sentences you add to answer that question. In this guide you will see what good commentary does, how to tell it from a repeat, and how to spot a paragraph where the explanation is missing.

points.heading: Commentary answers “So what?”
points.explanation: Look at this evidence: According to Torres, Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time moved later. A reader might wonder whether half an hour is a lot, or what it has to do with school time. Those gaps are what commentary fills. Without it, the reader has to guess how the evidence connects to the claim, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”

points.heading: Three jobs of good commentary
points.explanation: Good commentary does three things. First, it says what the evidence shows. Second, it says why that matters. Third, it ties back to the claim in your own words. Three sentence starters can help: “This shows that...”, “This matters because...”, and “So a later start would...”. Here is a model for the Seattle evidence: “The extra sleep matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours each night, and sleeping longer brings them closer to that amount. This supports starting school later because the Seattle result suggests that changing the schedule can help students get more rest.” Notice that the second sentence does not copy the claim word for word.

points.heading: Commentary must add thinking
points.explanation: Commentary is not a repeat of the evidence, and it is not a repeat of the claim. Suppose a writer adds these sentences after the Seattle evidence: “Students slept more in Seattle. They slept longer on school nights.” That only says the evidence again, so the explanation is still missing. Real commentary uses words like “because” or “so” to show your thinking. A sentence after the evidence is not commentary just because it is there.

points.heading: Match commentary to the claim, and check for gaps
points.explanation: Different evidence connects to different claims. The Seattle result supports Torres’s claim about sleep. Okafor’s bus costs support his claim about new problems. For example: According to Okafor, a district might need to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. Commentary: “If the district buys more buses, it has less money available for teachers or books. This supports examining transportation costs before changing the start time because the change could reduce money available for classroom needs.” To check a paragraph, ask one question after the evidence: does the writer say why it matters to the claim? If not, the explanation is missing. The same test works on a recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics. Strong commentary says that doctors who study children’s health agree, so the claim is not just opinion. Weak commentary only repeats the recommendation.

l_1ff6851c1953.title: Answering a counterclaim
l_1ff6851c1953.summary: Students identify the strongest opposing point in the other article and practice acknowledging it and responding with a rebuttal.
readings: A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems, by Daniel Okafor

segments.title: Who admits the other side?
segments.description:
Display two sentences from Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later: “Some people say a later start would cause problems with buses, sports and after-school jobs. Those problems are real, but they can be solved.”
Students reread them with their annotated copies and underline the words where Torres admits the other side has a point.
Name this move for the class: Torres is answering a counterclaim, a point the other side makes against her claim, like the problems Okafor raises.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: students underline “Those problems are real.” Say that Torres’s second sentence is her own opinion and needs support, which today’s rebuttals will add. Students used these annotated copies in earlier lessons, so have them out.

segments.title: Acknowledge, rebut, link back
segments.description:
Project Okafor’s transportation point as the counterclaim to Torres’s claim, and build the answer in three labeled moves.
Acknowledge: “Okafor is right that many districts run the same buses on several routes, so a later high school start could force other changes.”
Rebut: “However, a scheduling problem is not a reason to keep a schedule that leaves teenagers short on sleep. According to Torres, when Seattle high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
Link back: “That measured benefit is why our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, and then plan its bus routes around it.” Students label each move on their copy of the model.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not use Torres’s California sentence here. It shows a state required the change, not that districts solved bus costs. The rebuttal concedes the cost is real and weighs it against the Seattle result. Seattle shows only a sleep gain. Common mistake: dismissing the objection.

segments.title: Is this counterclaim fair?
segments.description:
Pairs get four one-sentence summaries of Okafor’s points on a handout. Beside each, they write Fair or Unfair.
They rewrite each Unfair sentence so Okafor would agree with it.
Then they say why a fair statement matters: a rebuttal to a twisted point does not answer the real one.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Okafor says a later high school start could require more buses and drivers, or make younger children start earlier. Fair.
2. Okafor says teenagers do not need much sleep. Unfair: he says they need 8 to 10 hours.
3. Okafor says school must never change its start time. Unfair: he says to weigh the costs first.
4. Okafor says a later end would leave sports teams less daylight to practice. Fair.

segments.title: Answer the other side to my claim
segments.description:
Each student takes out their revised claim, reasons sheet and annotated articles from earlier in the unit.
They choose the strongest point from the other article and write it as a counterclaim in one fair sentence.
Below it they write an acknowledgment, a rebuttal and a link back, using the three moves from the model.
They keep the sheet in their folder for the planning organizer.
segments.teacherNotes: Students arguing for a later start answer Okafor. Students arguing against answer Torres, often her Seattle result, and may reply that one city’s result may not transfer. Mistake: rebutting a different point than the one stated. Circulate and check the counterclaim sentence first. This feeds the organizer and drafts component.

segments.title: Partner test for rebuttals
segments.description:
Write three questions on the board: Does it state the other side fairly? Does the rebuttal answer that same point? Does the link back return to my claim?
Partners swap sheets and answer each question with Yes or Not yet, and give one suggestion.
Students revise one sentence on their own sheet using the feedback.
segments.teacherNotes: Model one Not yet aloud, such as a rebuttal that repeats the claim instead of answering the point. Ask for a specific suggestion, not “good job.” Rebuttals may stay as drafts, since students will assemble them in the organizer.

segments.title: Exit check: state the counterclaim
segments.description:
Display this passage from Okafor’s article: “Schools can teach students about sleep and why it matters. Families can set limits on phones and screens at night... These steps cost little and do not require changing the schedule for an entire community.”
On an exit slip, each student writes this counterclaim in one fair sentence, in their own words.
Students hand in the slip.
segments.teacherNotes: Strong answer: Okafor says there are cheaper ways to help students sleep, such as sleep lessons and screen limits, so the schedule need not change. Weak: “Okafor hates later start times” or copying the passage. Use the slips to see who needs help stating counterclaims fairly.

segments.title: What the organizer needs
segments.description:
Remind students that their claim, reasons, cited evidence, commentary and now their answer to the other side are all drafted.
Next time they will place each piece in a planning organizer.
Students keep today’s sheet with their other drafts.

keyIdeas: A counterclaim is the strongest point on the other side. A writer states it fairly, in the opponent’s own meaning, before answering it.
A strong answer has three moves. Acknowledge the point is real, rebut it with a reason or evidence, then link back to your own claim.
A rebuttal answers the point that was stated. It does not change the subject or wave the point away.
A rebuttal must not claim more than its evidence shows. The Seattle result shows students slept more. It does not show that bus costs were solved.
Answering the other side makes an essay more convincing. Readers trust a writer who shows they understood the opposing view.

Project a blank organizer with six boxes: claim, introduction notes, reason 1 chain, reason 2 chain, counterclaim response, conclusion notes.

segments.teacherNotes:

points.heading: Know what goes in each box
points.explanation: Each box on the organizer becomes a part of your essay. The claim and the introduction notes belong in the introduction. Each reason chain becomes a body paragraph. The counterclaim response becomes another body paragraph. The conclusion notes guide your conclusion. Keep the introduction and conclusion notes to short phrases, not full sentences. For example, introduction notes on Torres’s side might read: hook on teenagers dragging out of bed before sunrise; many are tired for biological reasons; claim last. points.heading: Build a chain for each reason
points.explanation: Every reason gets its own chain: the reason, evidence from an article with a signal phrase, and commentary that links back to the claim. Example: the reason is that students sleep more when school starts later. The evidence is: Torres reports that after Seattle moved from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, researchers found students slept a little more than half an hour longer. The commentary is: a later start added real sleep, not just a later bedtime. Notice that the commentary explains why the evidence supports the claim that our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

points.explanation: Evidence has to fit the reason, not just the topic. It is about sleep, so it is easy to match it with the reason that teenagers need more sleep than most get. But that fact shows sleep gained after a schedule change. Display two possible openings for the same essay on school start times.

segments.title: Model introduction: hook, background, claim

Claim: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because a later start gives students more sleep and a better chance to learn.”
Show the whole essay map: introduction, two reason paragraphs, one counterclaim paragraph, conclusion. Point out that the claim comes last in the introduction so the body paragraphs follow it.
segments.teacherNotes: Ask: which sentence could be moved without hurting the paragraph? Expected: none, because the order moves from interest to information to position. Mistakes: background that argues instead of informing; a hook that opens with “Since the beginning of time”; an invented statistic as a hook. Show a question or a true fact as other hook types.

Students take out their planning organizer and open the claim box and the introduction notes box.

segments.teacherNotes: Circulate and check the claim is last and the hook points at start times. Pro-later-start writers can use Torres’s sleep need; against writers can use Okafor’s point that students’ sleep matters. Common mistakes: hook is too general, background copies source wording without quotation marks or attribution, claim is buried mid-paragraph. Students keep the draft in their folder; it counts later toward Organizer and drafts.

segments.title: The parts of a conclusion
segments.description:
Project the model conclusion and label its three moves.
Restate: “A school day that begins no earlier than 8:30 a.m. would let students rest and be ready to learn.”
Synthesize: “Teenagers’ body clocks run later, and Seattle’s high schools showed that a later bell meant more sleep. The costs of buses and schedules are real, but they call for careful planning, not for leaving students tired.”
Closing thought: “A school that expects students to arrive ready to learn can start by letting them wake up rested.”
segments.teacherNotes: Compare restatement with the introduction claim: same position, new words and sentence shape. Synthesis uses only points the model’s organizer already supports; it does not claim the Seattle result solved bus costs. Mistakes: copying the claim after “In conclusion”, adding new evidence, ending with “Thank you for reading”.

segments.title: Draft my conclusion
segments.description:
Students open the conclusion notes box on their organizer.
They write a closing paragraph of three to four sentences: the claim restated in new words, one sentence that brings their points together, and a closing thought.
They compare their restatement with their introduction claim and reword it if the two match.
segments.teacherNotes: Check that each synthesis sentence comes from points already in their organizer, and that any line about the other side claims no more than the evidence shows. Prompt: what would a reader still remember tomorrow? Mistakes: new evidence, a vague closing such as “Sleep is important”. Students keep the draft in their folder; it counts later toward Organizer and drafts.

segments.title: Exit check: which sentence restates the claim?
segments.description:
Display four possible first sentences for a conclusion. The introduction claim stays on the board.
Students write the letter of the one that restates the claim in new words and give one reason in a short sentence.
Collect the slips on the way out.

Items:
A. “In conclusion, our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later because students need more sleep.” Wrong: copies the claim’s wording.
B. “A school day that begins no earlier than 8:30 a.m. would let students rest and be ready to learn.” Correct: same position, new words.
C. “Thank you for reading my essay.” Wrong: no claim.
D. “Sleep is important.” Wrong: too vague to restate the claim.

A conclusion restates the claim in new words, pulls together points the essay already proved, and ends with a closing thought. It does not add new evidence or repeat the introduction word for word.

The planning organizer feeds both paragraphs: the introduction notes and claim box shape the opening, and the conclusion notes box shapes the closing. A conclusion only uses points the essay has already supported.

segments.title: Write the chain from memory
segments.description:
Students take out their planning organizer.
On a slip, they write the links of a supporting-reason chain in order from memory.
They then check the slip against the organizer boxes.
Tell them that today the chain becomes a real paragraph.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected order: reason, evidence with a signal phrase, commentary, link back to the claim. Common mistake: placing commentary before the evidence, or leaving out the link back.

segments.title: Label a model body paragraph together
segments.description:
Project the model paragraph on Seattle sleep and read it aloud.
Introduce body paragraph and topic sentence, and explain that the topic sentence is the reason written as a full sentence.
Label each sentence with the class in four colors: topic sentence, evidence, commentary, link back.
Ask students to point to the signal phrase and to the words that return to the claim.
segments.teacherNotes:
Model, with labels:
1. A later start would help students get more of the sleep they need. (topic sentence)
2. According to Torres, after Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, University of Washington scientists found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. (evidence)
3. Half an hour every school night adds up to more than two hours of extra sleep in a five-day week. (commentary)
4. That extra rest brings tired teenagers closer to the 8 to 10 hours that sleep experts say they need. (commentary)
5. A later start therefore gives students more of the sleep they need, which is why our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. (link back)

points.heading: Build the counterclaim paragraph in four moves
points.explanation: A counterclaim paragraph uses the moves you learned for answering a counterclaim: state the other side fairly, acknowledge it, rebut it with cited evidence and commentary, then link back to your claim. Start by stating the other side’s point without twisting it. For example: “Daniel Okafor argues that a later start would strain transportation, because the same buses serve several schools and a district might have to buy more buses and hire more drivers.” Then acknowledge it: “This concern is real.” Next, rebut with evidence from the articles and explain how it supports your answer. End by linking back to your claim, such as “which is why our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Write your own sentences. Do not copy the model. If you chose a different point from Okafor, such as after-school jobs or other ways to help sleep, answer that point instead.

points.heading: Do not claim more than your evidence shows
points.explanation: A strong rebuttal is honest about what the evidence can and cannot prove. California’s 2019 law shows that a state required later start times: most public high schools can start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. It does not show how districts handled bus routes or costs. So the model paragraph says Torres’s article “does not say how districts have handled it.” It admits what is still unknown, then points to what the evidence does show: when Seattle high schools started later in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. The paragraph never says the bus problem is solved. Common mistakes to check for in your own draft are an unfair summary of Okafor, a rebuttal that changes the subject, and a rebuttal that claims Seattle solved bus costs. Ask yourself: what does my evidence actually show? Also check that your evidence has a signal phrase, such as “Torres reports that.”

points.heading: Use transitions to join paragraphs
points.explanation: A transition is a word or phrase that tells the reader how one idea connects to the next. Transitions work at the opening and ending of paragraphs, and they show a change, such as moving from a reason to the other side. When the first sentences of an essay have no transitions, it sounds like five separate pieces. Use this bank: “First,” opens the first reason paragraph. “Second,” opens the second reason paragraph. “Some people argue that” opens the counterclaim paragraph. “Still,” turns from acknowledging the other side to the rebuttal. “In short,” opens the conclusion. For example, “Some people argue that a later start would strain bus schedules” tells the reader that the essay is now turning to the other side. Do not use one phrase in every paragraph, because overusing it makes writing sound repetitive.

points.heading: Assemble a complete first draft

Add transitions where they are needed to connect the body paragraphs and the conclusion. Then check that your claim is the last sentence of the introduction and that the conclusion restates it in new words. A quick test is to have a partner read only the first sentence of each paragraph aloud. The five sentences should sound like one argument moving forward: an opening about school start times, two supporting reasons, the other side’s point, and the beginning of the conclusion. segments.title: The argument checklist and the marks we use
segments.description:
Project the argument checklist and read its five items aloud. Introduce peer review, argument checklist and feedback. Link each item to what students drafted in their essays, such as the signal phrase and the commentary.
Show the margin marks: a tick for done, a question mark for unclear or missing, +E for needs more explanation, and n/a for an item that belongs in another paragraph.
Show the feedback frame: one strength, then two suggestions. Each suggestion names a paragraph and says how to fix it.
segments.teacherNotes:
Checklist items:
1. Claim: the introduction ends with a clear claim someone could disagree with.
2. Evidence: each piece of evidence comes from an article and names the writer.
3. Explanation: commentary after each piece of evidence says how it supports the claim.
4. Counterclaim: the other side is stated fairly, acknowledged, and answered with cited evidence that does not claim too much.
5. Order and ending: paragraphs follow the introduction, two supporting-reason paragraphs, counterclaim paragraph, and conclusion order. Each supporting-reason paragraph starts with its reason; the counterclaim paragraph introduces the other side’s point. The conclusion restates the claim in new words, adds no new evidence, and ends with a closing thought.
Stress that checklist marks are not grades.

The class checks the claim item on the introduction only, then checks the second paragraph sentence by sentence for the evidence and explanation items. Mark in pencil as you go.
Students say aloud why each sentence earns a tick, a question mark or +E. Where an item cannot be checked in a paragraph, they write n/a.
segments.teacherNotes:
Sample draft, five paragraphs.
P1: Many teenagers drag themselves to school while their bodies still want to sleep. Schools have started early for a long time, but sleep science now questions that habit. Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
P2: Teenagers cannot get enough sleep when school starts early. Maya Torres writes that people from 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. She explains that a student who catches a bus at 6:45 a.m. would have to fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get even eight hours. Also, teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m. This shows that early schedules are a problem.
P3: Later start times also help students sleep more. According to Torres, when Seattle high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Torres adds, “They did not simply stay up later.” That is why our school should start later too.
P4: Some people, such as Daniel Okafor, argue that a later start would cost too much because buses make several trips each morning. That is a fair worry. Okafor writes that a district would have to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. However, California passed a law in 2019 that makes most public high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., so the costs must be easy to solve. Our school can fix its buses too.
P5: In conclusion, our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later because teenagers need more sleep and later starts help them get it. Students deserve a schedule that lets their bodies rest.

points.heading: The argument checklist and the marks
points.explanation: The checklist has five items: claim, evidence, explanation, counterclaim, and order and ending. Check each item in the paragraph where it belongs. The claim is checked on the introduction only. In a body paragraph, write n/a for that item. Use these margin marks: a tick for done, a question mark for unclear or missing, +E for needs more explanation, and n/a for an item that belongs in another paragraph. Example: in Marcus’s introduction, the last sentence, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later,” is a claim a reader could disagree with, so it earns a tick. Checklist marks are not grades.

points.heading: Spotting missing signal phrases and thin explanation
points.explanation: Evidence should come from an article and name the writer. Put a question mark where an evidence sentence has no signal phrase. In Marcus’s second paragraph, “Maya Torres writes” earns a tick. But “Also, teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m.” gets a question mark, because the fact is Torres’s and the sentence does not say so. Put +E wherever evidence has no commentary, or the commentary does not explain how it supports the claim. Marcus ends that paragraph with “This shows that early schedules are a problem.” That needs +E. It never links the 6:45 a.m. bus and the late tiredness around 11 p.m. to the need for eight hours of sleep. Also watch for claiming too much. In the fourth paragraph, “the costs must be easy to solve” claims more than the California law shows, so it gets +E too.

points.heading: Giving feedback that is specific and kind
points.explanation: Useful feedback names one thing that works, then points to a spot in the draft and says how to improve it. Use the frame: one strength, then two suggestions, each naming a paragraph and a fix. Compare two comments. “Good job. Fix the mistakes.” is vague. “Paragraph 2 names Torres, which helps. Add a sentence explaining why 8 to 10 hours of sleep matters for a student who must catch a 6:45 a.m. bus” names the place, gives a strength and shows the fix. A suggestion for Marcus’s conclusion could be: “Starting our school day at 8:30 a.m. or later would give teenagers a better chance to get the rest they need.” It restates the claim in new words instead of repeating the introduction. Never write on your partner’s words. The reviewer suggests and the writer decides.

points.heading: Turning feedback into a revision plan

If a suggestion is unclear, ask your partner a question. Your marked draft counts toward organizer and drafts. The final essay is graded later with the rubric. Peer marks are never scored.

segments.title: Revising is not proofreading

After: keep the first two sentences, then write: “Torres adds that they did not simply stay up later, so the later bell gave them real extra rest. For teenagers who need 8 to 10 hours, half an hour every school night is a real gain, which is why our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”

segments.title: What proofreading looks for
