Introduce proofread and conventions. Display three headings: spelling, punctuation, citation.
Under citation, list three checks: quotation marks open and close, a signal phrase names the writer, and the words in quotation marks match the article exactly.
Model proofreading by reading one sentence aloud and pointing with a pencil at each word.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students that a citation error can change meaning. Students should compare quoted words with the article, not with memory. Tell them spell-check misses words like ‘its’ and ‘it’s’.

segments.title: Fix the five sentences
segments.description:
Display five sentences, each with one error taken from the article topics.
Pairs find and fix each error and name its type: spelling, punctuation or citation.
Review the answers together and ask pairs to explain each fix.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Teenagers need more sleap than most of them get. Fix: sleep (spelling).
2. According to Okafor sports teams have less daylight for practice, especially in the fall and winter. Fix: comma after Okafor (punctuation).
3. Schools should start later because “doctors agree that schools should adjust.” Fix: add the signal phrase: Torres writes, “Doctors agree that schools should adjust.” (citation).
4. Torres writes that “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Fix: add closing quotation marks (citation).
5. Okafor argues that a plan that worked in Seattle may not work elsewhere, because each city has it’s own buses. Fix: its (spelling).

segments.title: Proofread my essay
segments.description:
Students proofread the whole essay one paragraph at a time, reading slowly with a pencil and checking each sentence.
They check every quotation against the article and mark each signal phrase.
They fix errors on the draft or on the final copy they will submit.
Students who finish early swap with a partner for a second read.
segments.teacherNotes: Provide both articles for checking quotations. Students may use a dictionary or spell-check, but remind them to read the essay once themselves. Tell students that a clean final copy is expected, whether it is typed or handwritten.

segments.title: Submit the final essay

Students check that their name is on the essay and that the essay is complete.
They submit the final essay in the way you have announced.
Each student writes on a slip one change that made the essay stronger, and hands it in with the essay.

Tell students the final essay is graded with the rubric and counts for 60% of the course grade. Do not promise extra class time unless it exists.

t_9cbdf7027e85.title: Save evidence for your essay
t_9cbdf7027e85.prompt: Use your annotated copy of Maya Torres’s article to save evidence you may use when writing your final essay. This is ungraded.
steps: Write Torres’s claim in your own words.

t_e2fc431b3182.prompt: What claim does Maya Torres make in the opening paragraph?

Students should learn more about sleep.
Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

t_ef80d43dad04.prompt: Which set gives Torres’s three main reasons for a later school start?

choices.text: Teens need more sleep; students slept more after a later start; sleep supports health and safety.

Students need later sports; Seattle changed its buses; California changed middle school times.
Teens need more sleep; families need new schedules; screens make it harder to fall asleep.

t_ef80d43dad04.explanation: Torres’s three reasons are that teenagers need more sleep, students sleep more when school starts later, and sleep supports health and safety as well as grades.

t_af24b83cd9fc.prompt: Which detail supports Torres’s reason that students sleep more when schools start later?

Seattle students slept over half an hour more.
Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.
Tired students have trouble controlling moods.

t_7e0558729b05.prompt: Give one fact or number from Torres’s article that a student could underline as evidence, and state which reason it supports.

t_1d96b9e6807c.prompt: The sentence “Many of them are not lazy” gives checkable evidence with a number.

choices.text: True
False

t_1d96b9e6807c.explanation: Torres’s statement that many teenagers are not lazy is an opinion, not a checkable fact or number.

t_5b720f6d611b.prompt: Daniel Okafor agrees that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, yet he argues that a later start is not an easy fix. Can a writer agree with the other side’s main fact and still argue against their conclusion? Use one underlined line from his article to back your answer.
followUps: Which sentence in Okafor’s first paragraph shows that he agrees about sleep? How does that agreement change the way you read the rest of his argument?
Okafor says of the Seattle result, ‘That is a real result.’ Why might a writer admit a point before answering it? Does it make you trust him more or less?
Would Torres’s argument be weaker if she had admitted the problems with buses and sports more openly? Why or why not?

t_7137977448bb.prompt: Torres gives experts, numbers and the Seattle results. Defend your view with a line from each article, and say what kind of evidence it is.
followUps: Okafor says Seattle is one city with its own buses, budgets and families. Is that a fair reason to doubt the study, or is it a way to avoid it? What would you need to know to decide?
Which of Okafor’s three problems (transportation, what happens after school, family schedules) could be checked with facts and numbers? What would you look for?
Does a possible effect count as evidence if no one has measured it yet? Where would you draw the line between evidence and opinion?

t_28c91a99ec15.title: Start an essay evidence list
t_28c91a99ec15.prompt: Ungraded preparation for the final essay. Make a tentative choice about whether school should start later, then connect it to details from the articles you discussed in class. Work on your own at home with your annotated articles.

t_d916592d1cf6.prompt: Which statement best gives Okafor’s claim?

choices.text: Schools should start at 8:30 a.m. or later to help students sleep.

Moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like.
Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.

t_8b43f2da87a4.prompt: Which set names the three problems Okafor raises?

choices.text: Sleep needs, student health, and school attendance
Bus routes, Seattle research, and screen use
Sports practice, homework, and student health
Transportation, after-school effects, and family schedules

t_a67464461b64.prompt: How do Torres and Okafor use the Seattle results differently?

choices.text: True
False

t_286baa0bf5a7.prompt: Name one kind of evidence Torres uses and describe how Okafor’s use of evidence differs.
t_286baa0bf5a7.answer: Torres uses expert statements, numbers or the Seattle results. Okafor mostly explains possible effects, such as problems with buses, after-school activities or family schedules, and gives few numbers.
t_286baa0bf5a7.explanation: Torres draws on experts, numbers and Seattle results, while Okafor mainly explains possible consequences.

t_b6e4e7558b07.prompt: Torres writes, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Okafor writes that “moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like.” Which claim is easier to argue for, and which is easier to argue against? Does being more specific make a claim stronger, or does it just give the other side an easier target?
followUps: Which exact words in Torres’s claim could someone disagree with? What would a reader who disagrees say?
Okafor’s claim is a real position, but what does it leave unsaid about what the school should do? How could you rewrite it so it names the action?
Think about “Our school should keep its current start time.” Is that as specific as Torres’s claim? Does it pass all three questions of the test?

t_8b27d89dc736.prompt: Take the statement “In 2016, Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.” It is true and it comes from an article about school start times, but it is not a claim. followUps: What would you have to add to this fact to turn it into a claim that takes a side?
Two students read the same Seattle fact. One writes a claim for a later start and the other writes a claim for keeping the current start. How can one fact support both sides?
Look at “Early school is bad.” It takes a side, so why does the test still mark it as vague? What question does it leave unanswered?

t_d1c392e36be9.title: Brainstorm reasons for your claim
t_d1c392e36be9.prompt: This ungraded note is a step toward your final essay. steps: Write the claim you revised in class. If you do not remember it, choose a side and write a specific claim about what our school should do.

t_be0be8d694ab.prompt: Which statement is a clear claim about what the school should do?

Our school’s start time is an important topic.
Our school should think about its start time.
Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

t_ea9cedf7d811.prompt: Which revision makes “A later start is bad” a specific claim someone could argue against?

choices.text: A later start can cause some problems.
A later start is a big problem for families.
Our school should not move its start time later.
Some families dislike a later start time.

t_ea9cedf7d811.explanation: This revision names the school and says what it should do. The other statements do not clearly state an action the school should take.

t_6a91482ec6df.prompt: Which statement reports a checkable event that could be used as evidence for a claim?

Seattle’s public high schools should start later in 2016.
Seattle’s public high schools had a better schedule in 2016.
Seattle’s public high schools started too early in 2016.

t_6a91482ec6df.explanation: This reports a checkable event described in Torres’s article. A fact can support an argumentative claim as evidence.

t_094ca03caa39.prompt: A claim becomes stronger just by getting longer, even if it does not say what the school should do.

choices.text: True
False

t_094ca03caa39.explanation: A strong claim can be short. It needs to take a side and clearly name what the school should do.

t_09a3e696e445.prompt: Revise “School start times are a problem” into a specific claim that names what the school should do.
t_09a3e696e445.answer: Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
t_09a3e696e445.explanation: This is one possible revision. Other answers are acceptable if they take a side, name the school, and state a specific action.

t_654dec56725d.prompt: A classmate says, “Many students like to sleep in on weekends” is a good reason for starting school at 8:30 a.m. or later, because it is true. Is a true statement always a good reason? Use the three questions from the reason test to decide, and explain which question the statement fails.
followUps: Which of the three questions does this statement fail, and how can you tell?
Can you change the statement so that it passes? What would you need to add to connect it to the claim that school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later?
Another card said, “Our cafeteria food is bad.” Does it fail for the same reason as the weekend card, or a different one?

t_81781c849fd6.prompt: Okafor’s three problems are transportation, after-school schedules and family schedules. Suppose a student who opposes a later start uses all three as reasons. Should you judge a reason only on whether it supports the claim, even if you disagree with the position? Why or why not?

t_46d1bf9eea2a.title: Strengthen your reasons at home
t_46d1bf9eea2a.prompt: This ungraded work helps you prepare for the Final essay. On a blank sheet, check that your claim has three distinct reasons that support it.

Cross out and rewrite any reason that fails a question.

t_cdda96237c3d.prompt: Which statement is a broad reason in Torres’s argument, rather than a specific piece of evidence?

Seattle students slept longer after the change.
Researchers measured students before and after the change.
Biology class grades went up after the change.

t_4be8ca1f77ca.prompt: A student proposes, “Our cafeteria food is bad,” as a reason school should start later. Why should the student reject it?

It is off topic and does not support the claim.
It is evidence that needs a source citation.
It says the same thing as another reason.

Reject it because it is about classroom seats.

t_d9c3fa3d1e0a.prompt: A statement can be true and still fail to support a claim if it is off topic.

choices.text: True
False

t_d9c3fa3d1e0a.explanation: A reason must relate to the claim and make a reader more likely to agree if it is true.

t_f37de3efd701.prompt: Name Okafor’s three distinct problems with a later school start that could support a student’s claim against changing the start time.

t_e30c38021f10.prompt: Torres writes, “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.” Another writer could paraphrase the sentences just before it in the same paragraph: “Torres explains that during puberty the body’s clock shifts later, so many teenagers are not sleepy until about 11 p.m.” Which version would you use in your essay? Would your choice change if your reason was about biology and sleep science, instead of about how unfair the schedule feels? Why?
If a reader saw the quotation without the words “Torres writes,” what would they not know, and why does that matter?

t_c074d99f4f4a.prompt: Here are two paraphrases of Torres’s sentence about the student who catches a bus at 6:45 a.m. and must fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get eight hours. Is changing an author’s meaning in a paraphrase as serious a problem as leaving out the author’s name? Which one would you trust less as a reader?

t_a79cc433b621.title: Practice citing one piece of evidence
t_a79cc433b621.prompt: Write one paraphrased sentence from “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that could support your final essay. This practice is ungraded.

t_374158bb3d35.prompt: Which sentence names the author, identifies who found the result, and includes the amount Torres reports about Seattle students’ sleep?

t_7be340cbbecc.prompt: When is quoting the strongest choice?

When Torres’s sentence needs a few words changed to sound simpler.
When Torres’s idea needs a different meaning to support a claim.
When Torres’s exact comparison is the important part of the evidence.

choices.text: True
False

t_ca69e8b49a7c.prompt: Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Is that enough to support her claim that our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later? Decide where you stand, and use your commentary sentences to defend your position.

If you were Torres, which piece of commentary would you add to make half an hour of sleep feel important to a skeptical reader?

t_4cbea1003cc9.prompt: Two commentary sentences can sound smart and still fail. Compare these: “Students slept more in Seattle. They slept longer on school nights.” and “This matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours, and 30 more minutes moves them closer to that.” What exactly makes one of them real commentary and the other not? Could a writer fake commentary without really explaining anything?
followUps: Which of the three jobs does each sentence do: say what the evidence shows, say why it matters, or tie back to the claim? What is missing from the weaker one?
Okafor’s bus costs and Torres’s Seattle result support opposite claims. Can the same habit of explaining work for both writers? What stays the same in their commentary, and what changes?
When you read a partner’s commentary, how can you check it against the writer’s claim and not your own opinion about school start times?

t_a0a1a9180214.title: Explain the Seattle result
t_a0a1a9180214.prompt: This is an ungraded step toward your final essay. Use the evidence and claim below to write two commentary sentences in your own words.
steps: Claim: Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

t_c4b99c842bb7.prompt: Torres says Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time changed. Which commentary best explains how this evidence supports Torres’s claim?

choices.text: The extra sleep happened in Seattle, where the high schools changed their start time in 2016.

t_c4b99c842bb7.explanation: This commentary says why the extra sleep matters and connects the result to Torres’s claim about a later start.

t_3e3739b1be2d.prompt: A paragraph says, “According to Torres, Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.” It then says, “Another reason is that tired students struggle to pay attention.” What is missing?

choices.text: A second piece of evidence about students’ attention in class
An explanation of how the Seattle result supports the paragraph’s claim

A conclusion that repeats the claim about students’ attention

t_ae42f8d13868.prompt: Okafor says a district might need to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. Which commentary explains why this evidence supports Okafor’s concern about the costs of a later start?

Several bus trips show that districts have enough buses already.
Bus costs show that Seattle students slept longer at night.
Buying buses could leave less money for teachers or books.

t_ae42f8d13868.explanation: This explains why the possible bus purchases matter to Okafor’s concern about the schedule change’s costs.

t_ccd16f28f34e.prompt: Torres says Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time changed. Write two sentences of commentary in your own words: explain why the extra sleep matters, then connect it to Torres’s claim about a later start.
t_ccd16f28f34e.answer: The extra sleep matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours each night, and more sleep brings them closer to that amount. This supports Torres’s claim because the Seattle result suggests that a later start can help students get more rest.
t_ccd16f28f34e.explanation: A strong response explains why the result matters and then links it to Torres’s claim without simply repeating the evidence or claim.

t_916ed14b029e.prompt: Any sentence that comes after evidence counts as commentary, even if it only repeats the evidence.

choices.text: True
False

t_916ed14b029e.explanation: Commentary adds the writer’s thinking about why the evidence matters and how it supports the claim; repeating the evidence does not explain that link.

t_9e6b686cdb18.prompt: Okafor says a later start would force a district to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or make younger children start earlier. The model rebuttal from class answers that a scheduling problem is not a reason to keep a schedule that leaves teenagers short on sleep, and it points to Torres’s Seattle evidence: students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Is that a strong rebuttal? Argue whether weighing a real cost against a measured sleep gain actually answers Okafor’s point, or whether it only sidesteps it.
followUps: What exactly did the Seattle result show, and what did it not show about bus costs? How far can a rebuttal go before it claims more than its evidence supports?
If you think the rebuttal falls short, what would you change in the acknowledgment, the rebuttal or the link back to make it answer Okafor’s actual point?
Would a reader trust the writer more or less because the rebuttal admits that the cost is real? Explain your reasoning.

t_66fdebe5c587.prompt: Okafor suggests cheaper steps instead of changing the schedule: teaching students about sleep, setting limits on phones and screens at night, and making sure homework does not keep students up late. A classmate says this is the strongest point against a later start. Another says it is easy to answer. Which view do you agree with, and what would you say back to Okafor without twisting what he actually said?
followUps: Before you answer, say Okafor’s point in one sentence that he would agree with. What would make that sentence unfair to him?
Does a rebuttal that says ‘teenagers’ bodies run on a later clock’ answer his point, or does it change the subject? How could you tie it back to his suggestion about screens?
Which of the three moves, acknowledge, rebut or link back, is hardest to do well when you disagree with a point? Why?

t_95fad09aed7d.prompt: Which sentence states Okafor’s transportation point fairly?

choices.text: Okafor says districts can change bus routes without added costs or schedule changes.
Okafor says teenagers need less sleep when buses pick them up early.
Okafor says later starts could require more buses and drivers or make younger students start earlier.
Okafor says schools must keep current start times because bus routes cannot change.

t_95fad09aed7d.explanation: Okafor says districts may need more buses and drivers, or younger children may have to start earlier.

t_d1ca8c56d66c.prompt: A rebuttal should answer the same opposing point named in the counterclaim.

choices.text: True
False

t_d1ca8c56d66c.explanation: A rebuttal responds to the point the writer stated, rather than changing the subject or dismissing it.

t_5d5912f5e82d.prompt: Which sequence uses the three moves in a strong answer to a counterclaim?

choices.text: Acknowledge the point, rebut it with a reason or evidence, then link back to your claim.
State your claim, repeat the counterclaim, then add a different reason.
Rebut the point, link to your claim, then acknowledge it is real.
Acknowledge the point, restate it, then end without returning to your claim.

t_5d5912f5e82d.explanation: The answer first recognizes the opposing point, responds with support, and connects the response to the writer’s claim.

t_54a36e074033.prompt: In one fair sentence and in your own words, state Okafor’s counterclaim that schools can help students sleep without changing the schedule.
t_54a36e074033.answer: Okafor says schools can teach students about sleep and families can limit screens, so the schedule may not need to change.
t_54a36e074033.explanation: A fair counterclaim captures Okafor’s point about sleep lessons and screen limits without claiming he opposes every schedule change.

t_a628bbd46413.prompt: Which statement about the Seattle result stays within what the evidence shows?

choices.text: Students slept a little more than half an hour longer; the result proves bus costs were solved.
Students slept a little more than half an hour longer; the result does not show that bus costs were solved.
Students slept almost an hour longer; the result does not show that bus costs were solved.
Students slept a little more than half an hour longer; the result proves every district would benefit.

t_a628bbd46413.explanation: The Seattle finding supports a sleep gain. It does not establish that bus costs were solved or that every district would have the same result.

t_c0289b6474d1.title: Polish your counterclaim response
t_c0289b6474d1.prompt: At home, make an ungraded draft for your final essay using the opposing point you chose in class.
steps: Write your claim and state the opposing point fairly in one sentence.
Acknowledge why that point matters, then answer that same point with a reason or evidence you remember from the articles.
Link your answer back to your claim. If you are unsure of an article detail, leave it out and check it against the article later.

t_00251cf5c731.prompt: Look at the model paragraph on Okafor’s buses. Sentence 3 reads: “If the high school starts later, something else has to change.” Some students say it is commentary because it sounds like a conclusion. Others say it is evidence. Decide which it is and defend your choice. What does the sentence do?
followUps: Does the sentence quote or paraphrase Okafor, and does it credit him? What would commentary have to do that this sentence does not?
Rewrite it so it becomes commentary. What words of your own would you add to explain why it supports the writer’s claim?
Is a sentence commentary just because it begins with because or so? Find one example in the model that shows the answer.

t_0cfe16184efe.prompt: The topic sentence of the Okafor model says a later start could force a hard choice about buses. A classmate says it should say a later start would cost the district a lot of money, because that is a stronger reason. Should the topic sentence be bold or careful? Argue your side using what the evidence actually shows.
followUps: What does Okafor’s evidence show about buses? Does it show that costs are certain, or that something has to change?
Is a stronger claim always a better one? What happens to a reader’s trust when the topic sentence promises more than the evidence can show?
Look at your own topic sentence from your draft. Does the evidence in that paragraph support everything it says, or only part of it?

t_b708dbec9464.title: Check your body paragraph chain
t_b708dbec9464.prompt: Prepare your body paragraphs for the final essay. This practice is ungraded.
steps: At home, reread your two body paragraphs and your claim.
Mark each sentence T for topic sentence, E for evidence, C for commentary, or L for link back.
Choose one commentary sentence. Rewrite it to explain how the evidence supports your claim, then underline the signal phrase in each paragraph.

t_258cde7d98b2.prompt: Which order matches the supporting-reason chain in a body paragraph?

choices.text: Reason, commentary, evidence with a signal phrase, link back
Evidence with a signal phrase, reason, link back, commentary
Reason, evidence with a signal phrase, link back, commentary
Reason, evidence with a signal phrase, commentary, link back

t_258cde7d98b2.explanation: The paragraph moves from its reason to credited evidence, then explains the evidence and links back to the claim.

t_cde5d23b15a4.prompt: In the transportation model, what part is this sentence: “This matters because one bus schedule links every school in the district, so moving the high school is not a change that stays in one building”?

choices.text: Topic sentence (T)
Evidence (E)
Commentary (C)
Link back (L)

t_cde5d23b15a4.explanation: The sentence explains why the transportation information matters to the writer’s argument. It does not quote or paraphrase Okafor’s article.

t_fc3fe3aa0c20.prompt: The Seattle study found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time changed. Which topic sentence promises only what this evidence can show?

choices.text: A later start would help students sleep longer.
A later start would improve every student’s grades.
A later start would solve the district’s bus problems.
A later start would make students healthier in every way.

t_fc3fe3aa0c20.explanation: The cited Seattle result supports a claim about students sleeping longer. It does not show that every student’s grades, bus problems, or health would improve.

t_8660eb782b08.prompt: The Seattle example shows that a later start solves every problem a school might face.

choices.text: True
False

t_8660eb782b08.explanation: The model does not say Seattle solved everything. Its evidence is about students sleeping longer, with some reported results in biology classes and first-period attendance.

t_f27478966e7c.prompt: Each supporting-reason box in the organizer, with its cited evidence, becomes one body paragraph; the counterclaim box is drafted later in the unit.

choices.text: True
False

t_f27478966e7c.explanation: Students use each supporting-reason box and its evidence to draft a paragraph. The counterclaim paragraph is not drafted in this lesson.

t_cea206a03d61.prompt: Daniel Okafor says a later start would strain transportation. In our model paragraph, the writer admits that Maya Torres’s article does not say how districts have handled bus routes or costs, and then points to the Seattle sleep gain. Does admitting what the evidence does not show make a rebuttal stronger or weaker? Take a side and explain why.
followUps: Which sentence in the model paragraph is the admission, and what would the paragraph lose if you deleted it?
Would a reader trust the writer more or less if the rebuttal claimed the bus problem was solved? Why?
What does the Seattle evidence actually show, and what does it not show about buses?

t_b522aa0eff02.prompt: Imagine a draft where all five paragraphs are strong but every one opens with the same phrase, or with no transition at all. Would you still say it is one argument moving forward? Which matters more in a first draft: strong paragraphs or clear connections between them? Defend your answer with the first sentences you heard read aloud.
followUps: When you heard only the first sentence of each paragraph, what did you expect the next paragraph to be about?
Why might “Still,” work better than “Some people argue that” at the point where the writer turns from the other side to the rebuttal?
If you could fix only one transition in your draft today, which one would help a reader most, and why?

t_f98a80a887e6.title: Plan one revision
t_f98a80a887e6.prompt: This ungraded at-home task will help you prepare your final essay. Use what you remember from your first draft. You do not need to look anything up.
steps: Write your claim about whether school should start later.
List the two reasons you used to support your claim.
Name the other side’s point that you answered.
Write one part of your essay you want to make clearer or stronger, and why.

t_43e88bc6e568.prompt: Which transition signals a turn from acknowledging the other side to the rebuttal?

choices.text: Second,
In short,
Still,
First,

t_43e88bc6e568.explanation: “Still,” signals a turn from the concern to the rebuttal.

t_0c9a63e9c60b.prompt: Which statement uses California’s law without claiming more than it shows?

choices.text: The law proves later starts solved routes and costs statewide.
The law requires later starts; it gives no route or cost results.
The law shows later starts raised grades statewide.
The law confirms all districts changed their bus schedules.

t_0c9a63e9c60b.explanation: Torres says California’s law requires most public middle and high schools to start later. The article gives no results about how districts handled routes or costs.

t_75a092101586.prompt: Which order joins the five paragraphs into a complete first draft?

choices.text: Introduction, counterclaim, first reason, second reason, conclusion
First reason, introduction, second reason, conclusion, counterclaim
Introduction, first reason, counterclaim, conclusion, second reason
Introduction, first reason, second reason, counterclaim, conclusion

t_75a092101586.explanation: The draft puts the introduction first, followed by both reason paragraphs, the counterclaim paragraph, and the conclusion.

t_b5149bed385a.prompt: In the model counterclaim paragraph, what does the writer acknowledge that Torres’s article does not explain about transportation?
t_b5149bed385a.answer: How districts have handled the transportation concern.
t_b5149bed385a.explanation: The model admits that Torres’s article does not say how districts have handled the transportation concern.

t_e3eb8c415809.prompt: A first draft should include all five paragraphs, even if some sentences are marked for revision.

choices.text: True
False

t_e3eb8c415809.explanation: The draft should be complete, but it does not have to be perfect. Writers can mark sentences to revise later.

t_83f709c947b3.prompt: Marcus’s sample draft says, “California passed a law in 2019 that makes most public high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., so the costs must be easy to solve.” The class marked this +E because it claims more than the law shows. Is that fair? Does one state passing a law prove that a school’s bus problems are easy to fix? Argue it with your partner, and say what Marcus could write instead.
followUps: Which words in the sentence claim too much, and what would you change them to?
Marcus’s sentence has no signal phrase. Would adding “Torres writes” fix the problem, or is the bigger problem the explanation? Why?
Okafor says a change that worked in Seattle might not work somewhere else. How could Marcus admit what is unknown and still point to the Seattle sleep gain?

t_45445efd1780.prompt: Marcus’s second paragraph cites Torres on 8 to 10 hours of sleep and a 6:45 a.m. bus, then ends, “This shows that early schedules are a problem.” Some students think the evidence is strong enough to speak for itself. Others say the sentence needs more. Decide where you stand. When you review a classmate’s draft, how much explanation is enough before you stop writing +E?
followUps: What would Marcus need to connect between 6:45 a.m., not feeling tired until around 11 p.m. and eight hours of sleep?
Does a reviewer who writes +E on a friend’s draft help the writer or hurt the friendship? What makes the difference?
Suppose a draft has no +E marks at all. What would you still look for in the commentary before you decide it is finished?

t_1004abe0d9c3.title: Prepare to explain your evidence
t_1004abe0d9c3.prompt: At home, use your marked draft to get ready to revise it next time. This is ungraded.
steps: Find one +E mark on your draft. If there is none, choose a piece of evidence whose connection to your claim could be clearer.
Write a note naming that evidence and explaining what your commentary needs to show about how it supports your claim.

t_e4b53966de09.prompt: Which comment gives a specific, kind suggestion a writer can use?

choices.text: Paragraph 2 names Torres; explain how the evidence supports the claim.
Paragraph 2 names Torres; add evidence from Okafor to that paragraph.
Paragraph 2 names Torres; move the claim from the introduction there.
Paragraph 2 names Torres; check every sentence for spelling errors.

t_e4b53966de09.explanation: The comment names a paragraph, points out something that works, and gives a concrete way to improve the explanation.

t_b0560e82bb82.prompt: In Marcus’s second paragraph, what mark belongs beside “This shows that early schedules are a problem”?

choices.text: A tick, because it follows the evidence.
A question mark, because it has no signal phrase.
n/a, because the item belongs in another paragraph.
+E, because it does not explain the evidence.

t_b0560e82bb82.explanation: The sentence does not connect the bus time and the time teenagers feel tired to the need for eight hours of sleep.

t_9f0aa394ba06.prompt: Where should a reviewer check the claim item on the argument checklist?

choices.text: On the first body paragraph, where evidence belongs.
On the introduction, where the claim belongs.
On the counterclaim paragraph, where the other side belongs.
On the conclusion, where the closing thought belongs.

t_9f0aa394ba06.explanation: The claim item is checked on the introduction. In other paragraphs, that item is marked n/a.

t_44752dfec9ba.prompt: A reviewer should mark +E beside evidence that has no signal phrase naming the writer.

choices.text: True
False

t_44752dfec9ba.explanation: Mark a question mark when an evidence sentence has no signal phrase naming the writer. Use +E when its explanation is missing or thin.

t_8ccbc7786bfc.prompt: Write two specific suggestions for Marcus’s second paragraph: one about its opening claim and one about explaining the evidence.
t_8ccbc7786bfc.answer: Soften the opening to say early schedules can make it harder for teenagers to get enough sleep. Add a sentence connecting the 6:45 a.m. bus and around-11 p.m. tiredness to the need for eight hours of sleep.
t_8ccbc7786bfc.explanation: Each suggestion names a place in the paragraph and gives a concrete change. The first avoids claiming too much; the second explains how the evidence supports the point.

t_d28ee8f47679.prompt: Daniel Okafor writes that the Seattle result is “a real result,” but says it comes from one city with its own buses, budgets and families. Does that point weaken the Seattle evidence, or does it only limit how far the evidence reaches? Take a side and use the three questions from today: Does it fit this reason? Does it give source clues? Could a reader check it?
followUps: Which source clues in the Seattle sentences (2016, Seattle, University of Washington, before and after) can a reader trace? Do those clues change when Okafor uses the evidence?

Torres uses the Seattle results to support “Students sleep more when schools start later.” Okafor uses them to show a limit. Is it fair for both writers to use the same evidence in different ways? Why or why not?
If a classmate says the Seattle finding is proven because both articles report it, what would you say? What would a reader need to check it?

t_70a04038787e.prompt: Look at the card “Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark.” and the card “That is why many teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m.” Neither names a source. Should both get the same label? Argue for your choice, and say whether you would feel differently if you agreed with the writer’s side.
followUps: What makes “many people think” different from a sentence that fits the reason but just does not name where it comes from?
Does the label depend on the evidence or on which side you are on? How can you check that you are labeling the evidence and not your opinion?
What kind of evidence would you still need to move the 11 p.m. sentence from Relevant only to Reliable?

t_4f892e3943d2.title: Build an evidence note for your essay
t_4f892e3943d2.prompt: At home, choose one reason you may use in your essay and build a short evidence note. Work on your own with your annotated articles.
steps: Choose one reason: teenagers need more sleep than most get; students sleep more when schools start later; or a later start would create transportation problems.

Use one matching detail: people ages 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep (Torres, the paragraph that begins “First”); Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time changed (Torres, the paragraph that begins “Second”); or many districts use the same buses for several school trips (Okafor, the paragraph that begins “The first problem”).
Write the reason, the evidence in your own words, and the article and paragraph where it appears. Add one sentence explaining how the evidence supports your reason.

t_41873f6c64e4.prompt: For the reason “Teenagers need more sleep than most get,” how should you label this evidence from Torres: “Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine say that people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.”

choices.text: Relevant only: it fits but gives few clues
Weak: it is an opinion with nothing to check
Reliable: it fits and gives source clues
Weak: it discusses a different reason

t_41873f6c64e4.explanation: The statement supports the reason and names a group, ages, and numbers. Those clues make it traceable, but they do not prove it is accurate.

t_af4767f50186.prompt: Which evidence best fits the reason “A later start would create transportation problems”?

choices.text: Games with schools on different schedules are harder to plan.
The same buses make several trips each morning.
Students need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night.
Parents leave for work early in the morning.

t_af4767f50186.explanation: This evidence describes how bus schedules could be affected. The other choices concern sports, sleep needs, or family schedules.

t_c39d4f9ec9e3.prompt: When evidence names a group, year, or place, the articles prove that it is accurate.

choices.text: True
False

t_c39d4f9ec9e3.explanation: Source clues help readers trace and check evidence. The articles alone cannot confirm its accuracy.

t_e4a08d16fb3b.prompt: Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Label this evidence Reliable, Relevant only, or Weak. Give two source clues and say whether those clues prove the finding is accurate.
t_e4a08d16fb3b.answer: Reliable. Source clues include Seattle, 2016, the University of Washington, and measurements before and after the change. The clues make the evidence traceable but do not prove it is accurate.
t_e4a08d16fb3b.explanation: The finding fits the reason that students sleep more when schools start later and includes clues a reader can use to trace it. Checking accuracy would require another source, such as the study itself.

t_4813ac2a70b1.prompt: For the reason “A later start would create transportation problems,” how should you label this evidence from Okafor: “Games against schools with different schedules become harder to plan.”

choices.text: Weak: it is about sports scheduling, not buses
Reliable: it fits and gives source clues
Relevant only: it fits but gives few clues
Weak: it gives a sleep finding instead

t_4813ac2a70b1.explanation: The sentence is about planning games, so it does not support the specific reason about transportation problems.

t_a71c3078049b.prompt: Look at the evidence card that says students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after Seattle’s change. Some people think it fits the reason that teenagers need more sleep than most get. Others think it fits the reason that students sleep more when schools start later. Which reason does it fit, and how can you tell? Then try this: what would the card need to say to fit the other reason?
followUps: What does the card show was gained, and which reason is about that gain?
Does the card tell us how much sleep teenagers need? What does the 8 to 10 hours card tell us that this one does not?
If a classmate put this card under the wrong reason, what test could you give them to check the match?

t_8b27b43a4d12.prompt: In the model organizer, the rebuttal to Okafor’s transportation point says Seattle shows the sleep benefit is real, and that neither article shows what bus changes would cost, so a district should plan for them, not give up. Is that a fair answer to his argument? Does it take the bus problem seriously, or does it dodge it? Decide where you stand and be ready to defend it.
followUps: Which part of the answer admits that Okafor’s concern is real? Which part pushes back on it?
What would Okafor say in reply? Does his reply change your mind?
How is this rebuttal different from one that changes the subject, and how could you check your own rebuttal for that mistake?

t_365e774e4392.title: Organizer and drafts
t_365e774e4392.prompt: Complete a one-sheet planning organizer for your five-paragraph argumentative essay on whether school should start later. Use your claim and work from earlier in the unit. Fill all six boxes: claim, introduction notes, reason 1 chain, reason 2 chain, counterclaim response, and conclusion notes. Give each reason its own evidence from one of the two articles, a signal phrase that names the writer or source, and commentary linking the evidence to your claim. State the other side fairly, then acknowledge it, rebut it with no more than the evidence shows, and link back to your claim. Keep introduction and conclusion notes as short phrases, not full sentences. This organizer is part of the graded Organizer and drafts component, worth 25% of the course grade.
steps: Gather your revised claim, reasons sheet, cited evidence with signal phrases, commentary, and counterclaim answer. Check whether you have each of these five items and tell a partner one gap.

Use the six-box model to sort your work. Put the claim and introduction notes in the introduction box; put each reason, its evidence, and its commentary in a separate reason chain; put the counterclaim response in its box; and put conclusion notes in the conclusion box.

Match each evidence card to the reason it fits and name its article. Check that the sleep-needs card fits the reason that teenagers need more sleep, while the Seattle sleep-gain card fits the reason that students sleep more when schools start later.

Fill every box on your organizer. For the counterclaim response, state the other side fairly, acknowledge it, rebut it, and link back to your claim. Use evidence that fits each reason, and keep the organizer to notes and drafted sentences rather than a full essay.

Swap organizers with a partner. Check whether every box is filled, each piece of evidence fits its reason, and the counterclaim response states the other side fairly. Star any box that needs work and write one word explaining why.
Take back your organizer, fix at least one starred box, circle the box that still needs the most work, and write one sentence explaining how you will fix it. Hand in the organizer.

t_2fa8223266e4.prompt: Which description correctly shows where the parts of the organizer go in the essay?

choices.text: The claim and conclusion notes go in the introduction; both reason chains become one body paragraph; the counterclaim response guides the conclusion.
The claim and introduction notes go in the first body paragraph; each reason chain becomes an introduction; the counterclaim response goes in the conclusion.
The claim and introduction notes go in the introduction; each reason chain and the counterclaim response become body paragraphs; conclusion notes guide the conclusion.
The claim and counterclaim response go in the introduction; reason chains guide the conclusion; introduction notes become the body paragraphs.

t_2fa8223266e4.explanation: The organizer maps the introduction, two reason paragraphs, counterclaim paragraph, and conclusion to their essay parts.

t_7a73661539dd.prompt: Which reason best matches evidence that sleep experts say people ages 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night?

choices.text: Students sleep more when school starts later.
Teenagers need more sleep than most of them get.
A later start creates transportation problems.
A later start reduces time for after-school activities.

t_7a73661539dd.explanation: The evidence is about how much sleep teenagers need, so it supports that reason. It does not show what happens after a schedule change.

t_90954083e9eb.prompt: Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after the start time changed. Which reason does this evidence best support?

choices.text: Students sleep more when school starts later.
Teenagers need more sleep than most of them get.
Later starts create transportation problems for districts.
Later starts reduce daylight for after-school practices.

t_90954083e9eb.explanation: The Seattle evidence describes sleep gained after the schedule change, so it fits the reason about students sleeping more when school starts later.

t_5c61b589c2b0.prompt: Okafor argues that later starts could affect bus costs and younger students. Which counterclaim response best follows the organizer’s three moves without claiming more than the evidence shows?

choices.text: Acknowledge bus costs are real; say California’s law proves buses will cost less; link the law directly to the claim.
Say bus costs are not real; use Seattle’s sleep findings to prove every district can afford the change; link back to the claim.
Acknowledge bus costs are real; repeat the transportation concern without answering it; end by restating the other side’s claim.
Acknowledge bus costs are real; use Seattle’s sleep findings to support the benefit; say the district should plan bus changes and link back to the claim.

t_5c61b589c2b0.explanation: The response acknowledges the concern, rebuts with evidence for the sleep benefit while calling for planning, and links back to the claim. The articles do not show what bus changes would cost.

t_3c9b5ccc0f91.prompt: Write one reason from the organizer model and give one piece of evidence that fits it, using a signal phrase to name its source.
t_3c9b5ccc0f91.answer: Reason: Students sleep more when school starts later. Evidence: Torres reports that after Seattle moved its start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, researchers found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.
t_3c9b5ccc0f91.explanation: The Seattle sleep finding matches the reason that students sleep more when school starts later. The signal phrase attributes the evidence to Torres.

t_0d4cefeeab78.prompt: Look back at the two openings from the start of class. Opening A says, “This essay is about school start times. I will tell you what I think.” Opening B says, “Imagine an alarm ringing at 6:00 a.m. while your body insists it is still the middle of the night.” Most of us picked B. Is a vivid hook always the best way to begin an argumentative essay, or can a plain, direct opening sometimes be stronger? Defend your view and name a reader or situation where the other choice would win.
followUps: What exactly does Opening B do that Opening A does not? Point to a word or phrase.
Imagine your reader is a school board member with ten essays to read. Would that change which opening you choose? Why?
Can a hook be too dramatic? Where would you draw the line between a vivid scene and an invented one?

t_30e2fcf88ce9.prompt: The model conclusion restates the claim in new words: “A school day that begins no earlier than 8:30 a.m. would let students rest and be ready to learn.” Option A copies the claim after “In conclusion.” Some people say a conclusion should repeat the claim exactly so the reader cannot miss it. Others say it should use new words. Which side do you agree with, and why? Think about what the reader gains or loses.
followUps: Compare the introduction claim with the restatement in the model. What stayed the same and what changed?
The model conclusion says the costs of buses and schedules are real but call for careful planning. Does that sentence help the argument or weaken it? Explain.
What would a reader still remember tomorrow from your conclusion? Is that the one thing you most want them to remember?

t_6fe9717ff29f.title: Polish your opening and closing
t_6fe9717ff29f.prompt: This ungraded practice prepares you for the Final essay. At home, use your own notebook to write a second version of your introduction and conclusion. Work on your own; you do not need classroom materials.
steps: Write an introduction of three or four sentences: open with a vivid scene, a question, or a well-established fact about school start times; add brief background; end with your claim.
Check that your hook leads to school start times and that your claim is the last sentence.
Write a conclusion of three or four sentences. Restate your claim in new words, bring together points your essay supports, and end with a closing thought.
Check that the conclusion adds no new evidence and does not repeat the introduction word for word.

t_12546f351af9.prompt: Which order should the sentences follow in an introduction?

choices.text: Background, claim, hook
Hook, background, claim
Claim, hook, background
Hook, claim, background

t_12546f351af9.explanation: The hook draws the reader in, the background gives needed information, and the final sentence states the claim.

t_9c98eab0432b.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest hook for an essay about school start times?

choices.text: Students have many different opinions about school and the choices they make each day.
School schedules have changed in different places at different times throughout history.
This essay will explain why I think school should start at a different time.
Imagine an alarm ringing at 6:00 a.m. while your body insists it is still the middle of the night.

t_9c98eab0432b.explanation: This vivid scene leads directly to the topic of school start times and helps the reader see why it matters.

t_906275e5ba66.prompt: Which set of moves makes a strong conclusion?

choices.text: Restate the claim in new words, connect supported points, end with a closing thought.
Restate the claim in new words, add new evidence, end with a closing thought.
Repeat the claim word for word, connect supported points, end with a closing thought.
Restate the claim in new words, introduce a new reason, end with a closing thought.

t_906275e5ba66.explanation: A conclusion restates the position, brings together points the essay has supported, and leaves the reader with a final thought without adding new evidence.

t_e94f6f990884.prompt: The last sentence of an introduction should state the claim.

choices.text: True
False

t_e94f6f990884.explanation: The claim belongs at the end of the introduction so it leads into the essay’s supporting paragraphs.

t_410263692410.prompt: The claim is “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because a later start gives students more sleep and a better chance to learn.” Write a first sentence for a conclusion that restates this claim in new words.
t_410263692410.answer: A school day that begins no earlier than 8:30 a.m. would let students rest and be ready to learn.
t_410263692410.explanation: This sentence keeps the same position while using new wording and sentence structure.

t_6229947dc09e.prompt: A classmate’s peer feedback says, “Say how this helps your claim.” You think your evidence already speaks for itself. Should the writer always follow peer feedback, or is the writer the final judge? Use the idea that feedback is a suggestion and the rubric levels (Excellent, Good, Developing, Beginning) to defend your view.
followUps: Think of the sentence about Seattle students sleeping a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. What would a reviewer need to see added before they stopped marking it +E, and would you reject that suggestion?
If you reject a suggestion, what reason would be strong enough? How could you check that reason against the rubric rather than just your own feeling?
When two peers give you opposite suggestions, how do you choose the one that would improve the argument most?

t_838dfcbb8f9e.prompt: You have ten minutes left before the essay is due. You could revise a paragraph with weak commentary, or you could proofread every quotation and signal phrase. Which should you do first, and which matters more to the final essay? Defend your choice.
followUps: Why is it a waste of time to fix commas in a paragraph you might still rewrite?

Look at this sentence: Torres writes that “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. What is wrong with it, and is that a revising problem or a proofreading problem? Could a small citation error change the meaning of what Torres actually said?
Can a student do both well in one session? What order would you use, and what would you skip if you ran out of time?

t_5071964b7ea2.title: Final essay
t_5071964b7ea2.prompt: Revise and submit a five-paragraph argumentative essay answering whether school should start later. State a clear, debatable claim; support it with reasons and cited evidence from both opinion articles; explain how the evidence supports your claim; address a counterclaim with a response; and include an introduction and conclusion. Revise one paragraph using peer feedback and the rubric, then proofread the essay for spelling, punctuation, and citation. The final essay counts for 60% of the course grade.
steps: Use the peer feedback, feedback sheet, and revision plan from last time. Choose the suggestion that would most strengthen your argument. You may reject a suggestion if you can explain why.
Revise one paragraph on your draft. Pay special attention to any +E or ? mark: add commentary explaining how the evidence supports your claim, or add a signal phrase that names the writer.
Check the revised paragraph against the rubric. Mark whether it fits Excellent, Good, Developing, or Beginning. If time allows, fix a second mark from the feedback sheet.
Proofread the essay one paragraph at a time. Read slowly, sentence by sentence, and read aloud if you can. Check spelling, punctuation, and citations.

Compare every quotation with the articles. Check that quotation marks open and close, the signal phrase names the writer, and the quoted words match the article exactly. Fix errors on your draft or final copy.
Check that your name is on the complete essay, then submit it as your teacher directs. Hand in a slip stating one change that made your essay stronger.

t_bce19a57754c.prompt: A peer marks +E beside the Seattle evidence and writes, “Say how this helps your claim.” What is the strongest revision?

choices.text: Add another Seattle detail without explaining how it supports the claim.
Correct the spelling and punctuation in the Seattle evidence sentence.
Remove the evidence and repeat the claim in different words.
Add commentary explaining that students slept longer and did not simply stay up later.

t_bce19a57754c.explanation: The +E mark signals that the paragraph needs an explanation of how its evidence supports the claim. The Seattle study found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights and did not simply stay up later.

t_35c9e9989fb0.prompt: Proofreading comes after revising and focuses on errors such as spelling, punctuation and citation.

choices.text: True
False

t_35c9e9989fb0.explanation: Revision strengthens the ideas and structure of the argument. Proofreading comes afterward to correct conventions, including spelling, punctuation and citation.

t_457ee660a19b.prompt: Which sentence correctly cites the Seattle evidence from Torres’s article?

choices.text: Torres writes that “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on weekends.”
Torres writes that “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
The article says, “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
Torres writes that students “slept about an hour longer on school nights.”

t_457ee660a19b.explanation: The signal phrase names Torres, and the quoted words match the article. The quotation marks open and close around the exact words.

t_516ca2909e98.prompt: A paragraph includes the Seattle sleep evidence but does not explain it. Write one sentence of commentary that connects the evidence to a claim for a later school start.
t_516ca2909e98.answer: This supports a later start because students slept longer on school nights without simply staying up later.
t_516ca2909e98.explanation: Commentary explains why evidence matters to the claim. The article reports that students slept a little more than half an hour longer and did not simply stay up later.

t_10070664d84b.prompt: Which proofreading change correctly fixes the citation in this sentence: Torres writes that “students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.

choices.text: Add a closing quotation mark after “nights.”
Add a comma after “writes” and leave the quotation open.
Replace the signal phrase with “the article says” and leave the quotation open.
Change “students” to “researchers” and close the quotation.

t_10070664d84b.explanation: A quotation needs opening and closing quotation marks. The quoted words should also match the article exactly.
