f_ff6d97a36315.question: What is the difference between a claim and a reason?
f_ff6d97a36315.answer: A claim is a position someone could disagree with, such as “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” A reason says why the claim is right, such as “Later starts help students get enough sleep.” A quick test: does the statement give a position on the policy, or does it explain why someone should accept that position? If it explains why, it is a reason.

f_f3f571be0fc0.question: Is a strong opinion the same as evidence?
f_f3f571be0fc0.answer: No. Evidence is a fact, example or expert statement that shows a reason is true. It answers the question “How do we know?” To test a statement, ask “Is this something that can be checked?” For example, researchers in Seattle found that students slept about half an hour longer on school nights after the start time moved. That can be checked, so it is evidence. “Everyone hates early mornings” is only an opinion.

f_ee6a271e7a09.question: Do I need real facts or numbers for my mini argument today?
f_ee6a271e7a09.answer: Not yet. You have not read the articles, so it is fine to say what kind of evidence would convince a doubter, such as “we could survey our grade.” Do not state made-up numbers as if they were real. Instead, say “Suppose a survey of our school found...” Later in the unit you will read both articles and choose real evidence from them.

f_3fb621856044.question: What is the difference between the claim and the reasons?
f_3fb621856044.answer: The claim is the position the writer wants us to accept. Torres states hers in the first paragraph: our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. The reasons explain why. Each one starts with a signal word such as “First,” “Second” or “Third.” Box only the claim itself, not the rest of the sentence, which previews the reasons.

f_db1ca3880b8e.question: What counts as evidence, and what does not?
f_db1ca3880b8e.answer: Evidence is something you could check: an expert statement, a time, a number or a study result. Examples are “8 to 10 hours of sleep every night” and the Seattle change from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. Opinions and appeals to feeling are not evidence. “Many of them are not lazy” is the writer’s opinion. “Those problems are real, but they can be solved” is a judgment, not a checkable fact.

f_268d2aaae0ec.question: Why do we use the same marks every time, and why keep the annotated article?
f_268d2aaae0ec.answer: Using the same symbols (box the claim, circle and number each reason, underline evidence) makes the argument easy to see again at a glance. You will use the same marks on the article against a later start. Keep your annotated copy in your folder. Later in the unit you will use it to choose evidence for your own essay.

f_7be27ed8285b.question: Does Okafor disagree that teenagers need more sleep?
f_7be27ed8285b.answer: No. He says teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and many get far less. He disagrees about the fix. He argues that moving the school day later would create new problems.

f_8276cf6436d7.question: Should I circle the Seattle paragraph as a fourth reason?
f_8276cf6436d7.answer: No. Okafor’s three reasons are transportation, what happens after school, and family schedules. The Seattle paragraph answers Torres’s evidence. Okafor admits the result is real, then says it came from one city and may not work the same way elsewhere. Bracket it instead of circling it.

f_7cda3b1a82a3.question: Why is Okafor’s claim harder to find than Torres’s?
f_7cda3b1a82a3.answer: Torres says directly that school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Okafor argues against a change, so his claim is less direct: moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like. He states it in the first paragraph and returns to it in the last.

f_32066d27551f.question: Both articles use the Seattle study, so how do they use it differently?
f_32066d27551f.answer: Both say students slept about half an hour more on school nights. Torres uses the result as evidence that a later start works. Okafor says it came from one city with its own buses, budgets and families, so it may not predict results elsewhere.

f_64644f3b2a7c.question: Is a longer claim a better claim?
f_64644f3b2a7c.answer: No. A longer claim is not automatically stronger. A claim gets better when it is exact. “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later” is short, but it names who should do what. Run it through the three questions: does it take a side, is it specific about who should do what, and could someone argue against it?

f_b3250b44be17.question: What is the difference between a fact and a claim?
f_b3250b44be17.answer: A fact reports something that can be checked. For example, “In 2016, Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.” is a fact from Torres’s article. A claim takes a position about what should happen, such as “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Facts do not take a side on their own, but they can support a claim as evidence.

f_455aacbb0a88.question: What if I change my mind about my side after reading both articles?
f_455aacbb0a88.answer: That is fine. Write the claim you believe now, not your first guess. Then test it with the three questions and revise it once. Make sure it names our school and states the action, either a time or keeping the current time.

f_919478016422.question: Does adding “I think” make my claim clearer?
f_919478016422.answer: No. “I think” does not change what the claim says. If “A later start is bad” is vague, “I think a later start is bad” is still vague. To fix it, say who should do what: “Our school should not move its start time later.”

f_6c110e48edcd.question: Is a reason the same thing as evidence?
f_6c110e48edcd.answer: No. A reason says why the claim is right, such as “Rested teenagers are safer drivers.” Evidence comes later and backs up a reason, for example something an article reports. If you write a reason that is only a number or a fact from the article, ask what point it makes about the claim and write that point as the reason. You will find evidence for each reason next time.

f_9270f9aea500.question: If a statement is true, why can it still fail the test?
f_9270f9aea500.answer: A true statement can still be off topic or fail to explain the claim. “The chairs are made of plastic” may be true, but it does not explain why students should choose their own seats. “Our cafeteria food is bad” is true for some students, but it has nothing to do with the start time. Truth is not enough. The reason must pass all three questions and it must make a reader more likely to agree.

f_787212774203.question: Do I have to agree with a reason to say it passes the test?
f_787212774203.answer: No. When you test a partner’s reasons, you judge only whether each reason supports the claim, not whether you agree with the position. You can also argue either side. Okafor’s three problems, transportation, after-school schedules and family schedules, are three different reasons for a student who opposes a later start. If two of your reasons say the same thing in different words, mark that as failing question 3.

f_8155a1c638a4.question: Do I need a signal phrase if I put the sentence in quotation marks?
f_8155a1c638a4.answer: Yes. Quotation marks show the words are exact, but they do not tell the reader who said them. Add a phrase such as Torres writes, then the quotation: Torres writes, “Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.”

f_59aafaa5d742.question: Is it a paraphrase if I just swap a few words in the sentence?
f_59aafaa5d742.answer: No. A paraphrase uses your own words and your own sentence shape. Changing a few words, such as “Torres says a student who has to catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. must fall asleep by 9:30 p.m. to get eight hours,” stays too close to the original. It must also still name the author.

f_cb755f10da0c.question: Can I make the paraphrase shorter or stronger so it sounds better?
f_cb755f10da0c.answer: Not if it changes what the author said. Read it, cover it, say it in your own words, then check the meaning against the original. “Torres says teenagers cannot sleep before 9:30 p.m.” changes the meaning. Torres says a student with a 6:45 a.m. bus would need to be asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get eight hours.

f_fb154a723da7.question: What is the difference between evidence and commentary?
f_fb154a723da7.answer: Evidence is the fact, quotation or paraphrase taken from an article, such as Torres saying Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Commentary is your own thinking after it. It says what the evidence shows, why that matters, and how it ties back to your claim.

f_bc2499f0a50d.question: Is it commentary if I just say the evidence again in different words?
f_bc2499f0a50d.answer: No. “Students slept more in Seattle. They slept longer on school nights.” only repeats the evidence. Commentary adds the link the reader is missing. Ask yourself, “So what? Why does this help the claim?” Then answer with “because” or “so”, for example: “This matters because teens need 8 to 10 hours, and 30 more minutes moves them closer to that.”

f_ba9ebe74e272.question: Can I copy my claim into my commentary to tie it back?
f_ba9ebe74e272.answer: No. Tie back to the claim in your own words. Do not copy it word for word. For example, instead of repeating “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later,” you can write, “So a later start would help students get the sleep they need.” The sentence starters “This shows that...”, “This matters because...” and “So a later start would...” can help you begin.

f_38332bc90691.question: Why do I have to say what Okafor believes before I answer him? Can’t I just argue my side?
f_38332bc90691.answer: A rebuttal only works if it answers the real point. If you twist his point, your answer misses it. Stating it fairly, in a way Okafor would agree with, also shows readers you understood the other side, and that makes them trust you more.

f_3844a96fe490.question: Can I use Torres’s California sentence to show that districts can solve bus costs?
f_3844a96fe490.answer: No. The California sentence shows that a state passed a law requiring later starts. It does not show that districts solved their bus costs. For the transportation point, use the Seattle result instead: when high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. That shows a sleep gain, so say only that. Then argue that a scheduling problem is not a reason to keep a schedule that leaves teenagers short on sleep.

f_4e2f9a2aacb8.question: What if I’m arguing against a later start? What do I answer?
f_4e2f9a2aacb8.answer: Answer Torres. Pick her strongest point, often the Seattle result. State it fairly, admit it is a real result, then rebut it. For example, you can say it comes from one city, so it may not work the same way in our school. Then link back to your own claim. Keep the same three moves: acknowledge, rebut, link back.

f_8eebb6c3165c.question: What is the difference between evidence and commentary? They both seem to be about the article.
f_8eebb6c3165c.answer: Ask what the sentence does. Evidence quotes or paraphrases facts or ideas from the article and credits the writer, as in “Daniel Okafor explains that many districts use the same buses for several trips each morning.” Commentary explains how that evidence supports your claim, as in “This matters because one bus schedule links every school in the district.” Using because or so does not make a sentence commentary. Check whether it gives the article’s information or your own explanation.

f_af62ac414326.question: Why does the topic sentence say “could” instead of “would”?
f_af62ac414326.answer: A topic sentence should promise only what the evidence can show. In the Okafor model, the evidence shows that buses would have to change if the high school starts later. It does not prove that costs are certain. “Could” says exactly that and no more. Before you write your topic sentence, look at your evidence and ask what it really shows.

f_68f02f203470.question: My commentary sounds like I am just repeating the evidence. How do I fix it?
f_68f02f203470.answer: Use the frames “This shows that ___ because ___.” Then ask yourself, “So what?” The commentary should explain why the fact matters for your claim. In the Seattle model, the evidence says students slept a little more than half an hour longer. The commentary adds that half an hour a night adds up to more than two hours over a school week. Your commentary should add a link in the reasoning that the article does not state. Note also that the model does not say Seattle solved everything. It says only that students got more sleep.

f_a5c78a3c6a77.question: What if my rebuttal says the bus problem is solved?
f_a5c78a3c6a77.answer: Do not say that. California’s 2019 law shows that a state required later starts. It does not show how districts handled bus routes or costs. Admit what is still unknown, as the model does with “does not say how districts have handled it.” Then point to what the evidence does show, such as the Seattle sleep gain of a little more than half an hour on school nights.

f_6a25b49caa9e.question: What if I chose a different point from Okafor, like after-school jobs or other ways to help sleep?
f_6a25b49caa9e.answer: Answer that point instead. Use the same four moves: state his point fairly, acknowledge it, rebut it with cited evidence and commentary, and link back to your claim. Ask yourself what your evidence actually shows, and do not claim more than that.

f_a0a3988c62a6.question: Do I need a transition at the start of every paragraph?
f_a0a3988c62a6.answer: No. Use transitions where they help the reader see how one idea connects to the next. Examples are “Second,” for the next reason, “Some people argue that” for the counterclaim, “Still,” to turn to your rebuttal, and “In short,” for the conclusion. Do not repeat one phrase in every paragraph. Your draft does not have to be perfect, but all five paragraphs must be there.

f_cf0998a2f033.question: Is the checklist a grade? Will my partner’s marks count against me?
f_cf0998a2f033.answer: No. Checklist marks are not grades. Ticks, question marks and +E marks are feedback to help the writer revise. Peer marks are never scored. Your marked draft counts toward organizer and drafts, and the final essay is graded later with the rubric.

f_e5e287faea97.question: Why does my partner put n/a next to the claim item on a body paragraph?
f_e5e287faea97.answer: Each checklist item is checked in the paragraph where it belongs. The claim item is checked on the introduction, so a body paragraph cannot show it. In Marcus’s draft, item 1 gets a tick in the first paragraph and n/a in the second through fifth.

f_a557e204ba91.question: When do I mark +E, and when do I mark a question mark?
f_a557e204ba91.answer: Mark +E where evidence has no commentary, or the commentary does not explain how it supports the claim. In Marcus’s second paragraph, “This shows that early schedules are a problem” gets +E because it never links the 6:45 a.m. bus and the late tiredness around 11 p.m. to eight hours of sleep. Mark a question mark where an evidence sentence has no signal phrase naming the writer, such as “Also, teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m.” The fact comes from Torres, but the sentence does not say so.

f_7daeac6311af.question: My partner gave me a suggestion I disagree with. Do I have to make that change?
f_7daeac6311af.answer: No. The reviewer suggests and the writer decides. If a suggestion is unclear, ask your partner a question. Then pick the suggestion that would improve your draft most and write your plan for it on the exit slip. You will make the revision next time.

f_ecf031145c9f.question: If the American Academy of Sleep Medicine statement has a named group, ages and numbers, does that prove it is accurate?
f_ecf031145c9f.answer: No. Those details are source clues. They show the statement comes from a named group of sleep experts that a reader could look up, so we call it reliable. But the two articles alone cannot confirm that it is accurate. To do that, you would need another source, such as the original study or report.

f_4e31de59e030.question: Is a piece of evidence weak if it is on the other side from my opinion?
f_4e31de59e030.answer: No. The label describes the evidence, not the side. Ask three questions. Does it fit this reason? Does it give source clues? Could a reader check it? Evidence can be reliable even if you disagree with it. It can be weak even if you agree with it.

f_9c65787899f4.question: Both writers use the Seattle results. Does Okafor’s point about one city cancel the finding?
f_9c65787899f4.answer: No. Okafor says, “That is a real result.” Both articles report that Seattle students slept about half an hour more on school nights. Okafor only limits how far the finding reaches. A change that worked in Seattle might not work the same way somewhere else. A limit on reach does not cancel the finding.

f_94a602c4f60a.question: Why does the Seattle card go with reason B and not reason A?
f_94a602c4f60a.answer: Reason A is about how much sleep teenagers need. The Seattle card shows students actually gaining a little more than half an hour of sleep after Seattle’s public high schools moved from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m. That is sleep gained after a later start, so it fits reason B. The card about 8 to 10 hours a night fits reason A.

f_2c3331ef2e94.question: My evidence is about the right topic. How do I know it fits my reason?
f_2c3331ef2e94.answer: Use the match test. Ask whether the evidence directly shows that the reason is true. A sentence about school start times is not enough. For example, the buses making several trips each morning fits a reason about transportation problems. It does not fit a reason about after-school activities, which needs evidence like less daylight for practice when school ends at 4:00 p.m.

f_1bf17f736f2a.question: Can I rebut Okafor’s bus point by saying California passed a law for later start times?
f_1bf17f736f2a.answer: No. The California law shows that a schedule change can be required. It does not answer the cost of buses. A better rebuttal stays on the point. Seattle shows the sleep benefit is real, and neither article shows what bus changes would cost, so a district should plan for them, not give up.

f_8ed6692c3aff.question: Can I start my introduction with a statistic or a big general statement?
f_8ed6692c3aff.answer: Only if it is a well-established fact and it leads straight to school start times. Do not make up a number to sound impressive. A general opener such as “Since the beginning of time” does not point to the topic, so it does not work. A vivid scene, a question or a true fact about teenage sleep all do.

f_673bd03c792c.question: Is it okay to copy my claim into the conclusion after “In conclusion”?
f_673bd03c792c.answer: No. The conclusion should restate the same position in new words and a new sentence shape. For example, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later” can become “A school day that begins no earlier than 8:30 a.m. would let students rest and be ready to learn.” Check your restatement against your introduction claim and reword it if the two match.

f_7f3b90468ef5.question: Can I add a new fact or example to my conclusion to make it stronger?
f_7f3b90468ef5.answer: No. The conclusion pulls together points your essay has already supported. Use only points from your planning organizer that you proved in the body. End with a closing thought that a reader will remember, not a vague line such as “Sleep is important” or “Thank you for reading.”

f_3c68062c1679.question: If I add a new quotation from an article, is that revising or proofreading?
f_3c68062c1679.answer: It depends on why you add it. Revising changes the argument, such as adding commentary that explains how the evidence supports your claim. Check the problem first. If a reviewer marked +E because commentary is missing, new evidence will not fix it. Proofreading only corrects spelling, punctuation and citation.

f_c140799263ce.question: What if I disagree with a peer’s suggestion?
f_c140799263ce.answer: That is allowed. Peer feedback is a suggestion, and the writer decides. Pick the suggestion that would improve your argument most, then check it against the rubric levels: Excellent, Good, Developing, Beginning. You may reject a suggestion if you can say why.

f_e57be8014e55.question: Why should I check my quotations against the article and not my memory?
f_e57be8014e55.answer: A citation error can change meaning. Compare each quotation with the article word for word. Check that the quotation marks open and close, that a signal phrase names the writer, and that the words inside the quotation marks match exactly. Spell-check will not catch these errors, or words like ‘its’ and ‘it’s’.

s_9b32ddcc66d8.title: Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later
s_9b32ddcc66d8.text:
# Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later

*By Maya Torres. An opinion article written for this unit; the writer is fictional, the facts are real.*

Every school morning, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed before the sun is up. Many of them are not lazy. They are tired, and science can explain why. Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because later start times help students sleep enough, learn better and stay healthier.

First, teenagers need more sleep than most of them get. Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine say that people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. A student who must catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. would have to fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get even eight hours. For most teenagers, that is not realistic.

The reason is biology, not bad habits. During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts later. The brain starts releasing melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, later in the evening than it did in childhood. That is why many teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m. Asking them to fall asleep earlier is like asking an adult to fall asleep at 7 p.m.

Doctors agree that schools should adjust. In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children's doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Yet a report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that fewer than one in five American middle and high schools started that late.

Second, when schools do start later, students really do sleep more. In 2016, the public high schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. Scientists from the University of Washington measured students' sleep before and after the change. They found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. They did not simply stay up later. In the biology classes the researchers studied, grades went up, and at one school, fewer students were late or absent from first period.

Third, sleep is about more than grades. Tired students have a harder time paying attention, controlling their moods and making safe choices. Teenagers who drive to school are safer behind the wheel when they are rested. Sleep also helps the body fight illness and helps young athletes recover.

Some people say a later start would cause problems with buses, sports and after-school jobs. Those problems are real, but they can be solved. Districts can change bus routes, and teams can adjust practice times. California has already done it: a state law passed in 2019 requires most public high schools there to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.

We expect students to show up ready to learn. The least we can do is give them a schedule that lets them get the sleep their bodies need. It is time to let us sleep.

s_80b53a33b05f.title: A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems
s_80b53a33b05f.text:
# A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems

*By Daniel Okafor. An opinion article written for this unit; the writer is fictional, the facts are real.*

Nobody wants exhausted students. Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and many get far less. But moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like. For many families and communities, a later start would create new problems that are just as serious as the one it tries to solve.

The first problem is transportation. Many school districts do not have enough buses and drivers to take every student to school at the same time. Instead, the same buses make several trips each morning: one for the high school, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. If the high school starts later, something else has to change. The district must buy more buses and hire more drivers, which costs money that could pay for teachers or books, or the younger children must go to school earlier. Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark.

The second problem is what happens after school. A later start means a later end. If school lets out at 4:00 p.m. instead of 3:00 p.m., sports teams have less daylight for practice, especially in the fall and winter. Games against schools with different schedules become harder to plan. Students who work part-time jobs to help their families would earn less. Others who care for younger brothers and sisters after school might not get home in time.

The third problem is family schedules. Many parents leave for work early. Right now, some can drop their teenagers off at school on the way. With a later start, those students might need to find another way to get there, or stay home alone in the morning. The change would affect far more people than just the students.

Supporters of later start times point to research. In Seattle, for example, high schools moved their start time almost an hour later in 2016, and researchers found that students there slept about half an hour more on school nights. That is a real result. But it comes from one city with its own buses, budgets and families. A change that worked in Seattle might not work the same way somewhere else.

There are also other ways to help students sleep. Schools can teach students about sleep and why it matters. Families can set limits on phones and screens at night, since the light from screens can make it harder to fall asleep. Teachers can make sure homework does not keep students up past midnight. These steps cost little and do not require changing the schedule for an entire community.

Students' sleep matters. But before our school changes its start time, we should look honestly at the costs to families, younger children and the whole community. A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves.
